Cooperative Intelligent Transport Systems · in depth When vehicles and roads talk to each other . C-ITS lets cars, trucks, bicycles, traffic lights and road operators exchange short wireless messages so everyone sees further than their own sensors. This guide explains the full European standards stack — from the radio bits up to the EU trust model — built from the primary ETSI, C-Roads, CAR 2 CAR and EU sources. Start: What is C-ITS? → The protocol stack 5.9 GHz Dedicated ITS band 5.855–5.925 GHz 1–10 Hz Awareness beacon rate adaptive CAM / VAM ≈300 m Direct V2X range line-of-sight, ITS-G5 / PC5 2 stacks ITS-G5 & C-V2X 802.11p vs 3GPP PC5 The core idea Every participant — a car, a roadside unit at a junction, even a cyclist's phone — is an ITS station running the same layered communication stack. Stations broadcast small, signed, standardised messages over a dedicated 5.9 GHz radio. A neighbour receiving them builds a live picture of its surroundings: who is where, moving how fast, and what hazards lie ahead — beyond line of sight and before any on-board sensor could detect them. The hard part is making this work between every brand of vehicle and every country's road operator. That interoperability is what the standards on this site exist to guarantee. Foundations What is C-ITS? Cooperative Intelligent Transport Systems (C-ITS) enable vehicles, road infrastructure, and network services to exchange secured, trusted messages in real time — without any prior knowledge of each other. The result is a shared awareness of the road that no single sensor can provide alone, enabling safety warnings, traffic efficiency services, and the stepping stone toward automated driving. ETSI TR 101 607 ETSI TR 103 903 Directive 2010/40/EU Directive (EU) 2023/2661 Definition and core concept The EU regulatory framework defines C-ITS as "intelligent transport systems that enable ITS users to interact and cooperate by exchanging secured and trusted messages, without any prior knowledge of each other and in a non-discriminatory manner" (Directive (EU) 2023/2661). In practice this means any compliant road user — a car, a truck, a motorcycle, a pedestrian with a phone — or any piece of road infrastructure can broadcast and receive standardised messages that all participants understand, verify, and trust. The broader term V2X (Vehicle-to-Everything) captures the full range of communication directions: V2V (vehicle-to-vehicle), V2I (vehicle-to-infrastructure), V2N (vehicle-to-network / cloud), and V2P (vehicle-to-pedestrian / vulnerable road user). C-ITS is the European standardised realisation of V2X, grounded in ETSI, CEN, and ISO specifications and backed by EU mandate M/453. ● The cooperative difference A camera or radar only sees what is in its field of view. A C-ITS station shares its own state — position, speed, heading, brake status, detected hazard — with every station within radio range, extending each participant's situational awareness far beyond its own sensors and around blind corners. C-ITS information sharing is classified as tactical when the information demands a direct course of action within around one second (e.g. emergency brake warning, intersection collision risk). It is strategical when the information is intended for awareness of a situation several seconds or more ahead (e.g. road works ahead sign, weather warning). Tactical information imposes stricter data-quality, latency, and security requirements; strategic information can tolerate slightly looser constraints and may travel via cellular or cloud paths. The problems C-ITS solves ~1.19 M Road deaths in EU (2001–2023) Road safety remains a top EU priority ~25 % Accidents at intersections Where V2I warnings add most value ~30 % CO₂ reduction potential From smoother, cooperative traffic flow Road transport faces two intertwined challenges: safety and efficiency . Human reaction time averages around 1.5 seconds; a car at 130 km/h travels 54 metres in that time. C-ITS compresses the effective warning window by delivering machine-to-machine alerts before a hazard enters the driver's field of view. Simultaneously, coordinated signal-phase information from traffic lights (via SPATEM/MAPEM messages) lets vehicles approach junctions at the right speed, reducing stop-and-go waves and therefore fuel consumption and emissions. Safety use cases Emergency Electronic Brake Light (EEBL) — V2V, <100 ms Intersection Collision Risk Warning (ICRW) Longitudinal Collision Risk Warning (LCRW) Road Hazard Signalling (RHS) — slippery road, obstacle Emergency Vehicle Approaching Vulnerable Road User (pedestrian, cyclist) warnings Efficiency use cases Green Light Optimal Speed Advisory (GLOSA) In-Vehicle Signage (speed limits, variable signs) Road Works Warning Probe Vehicle Data for traffic management Electric Vehicle charging spot notification Tyre pressure and tyre information services V2X communication directions V2V — Vehicle to Vehicle Direct short-range radio exchange between moving vehicles. The primary bearer is ITS-G5 (5.9 GHz, based on IEEE 802.11p/bd) or C-V2X (LTE/5G PC5 sidelink). No network infrastructure required; latency is typically under 10 ms over the air. V2I — Vehicle to Infrastructure Exchange between vehicles and Road-Side Units (RSUs) deployed at junctions, tunnels, variable message signs, or motorway gantries. RSUs bridge local radio with the road operator backend, enabling traffic management centre instructions to reach vehicles in real time. V2N — Vehicle to Network Cellular (3G/4G/5G) path to OEM backends, service providers, or central ITS platforms. Used for strategical information (map updates, weather, route-level hazards) and for C-Roads Hybrid deployments that carry C-ITS packets "sealed in an envelope" over IP networks. V2P — Vehicle to Pedestrian / Vulnerable Road User Warnings targeting pedestrians, cyclists, and power two-wheelers (PTWs). Covered by the Vulnerable road user Awareness Message (VAM) introduced in Release 2 (ETSI TS 103 300 series). ● Direct vs. indirect communications C-ITS direct communication is constellation-based : no dynamic network configuration occurs; ITS stations broadcast into the shared radio medium and every station within range can receive. This contrasts with IP-configured (indirect) networks used by DFRS, NAPCORE, and OEM cloud backends. For tactical safety data, the constellation model is preferred because it requires no prior connection setup. Actors in the C-ITS ecosystem The C-ITS ecosystem (as framed by ETSI TR 103 903) has a deliberately small number of active actors compared to the broader internet ecosystem. Each actor operates one or more ITS Stations (ITS-S) — the hardware/software component that implements the standardised protocol stack. 🚗 Vehicles (OBUs) On-Board Units in passenger cars, trucks, motorcycles, buses. The primary source of CAM (Cooperative Awareness Message) broadcasts at up to 10 Hz. OEM backends connect via V2N for software updates and map services. 🚦 Road-Side Units (RSUs) Fixed infrastructure at junctions, road-works zones, tunnels. Broadcast DENM hazard alerts, SPATEM signal-phase data, MAPEM intersection maps, and IVIM in-vehicle information messages. Typically operated by road authorities. 🏢 Central Stations Traffic management centres and road operator backends. Aggregate probe data, issue road-works warnings, manage the RSU network, and interface to national access points (NAPs) for SRTI (Safety Related Traffic Information). 🛣️ Road Operators Motorway and urban road authorities responsible for deploying RSUs, configuring C-ITS services, and complying with Directive (EU) 2023/2661. C-Roads is the EU coordination project for harmonised road operator deployment. 🔧 OEMs & Tier-1 Suppliers Vehicle manufacturers implementing OBU hardware and software to C-Roads / C2C-CC profiles. Responsible for certificate provisioning via the EU CCMS (C-ITS Security Credential Management System) and for vehicle type approval. 🚶 Vulnerable Road Users Pedestrians, cyclists, and PTW riders. Their devices (smartphones, smart helmets) act as ITS-S stations, sending VAM messages and receiving hazard alerts in Release 2. Service deployment phases: Day-1, Day-1.5, Day-2 The industry and regulators have structured C-ITS service rollout into phased "Days" that reflect increasing capability, complexity, and automation level: 1 Day-1 — Cooperative awareness and hazard warning : The foundational services standardised in Release 1. Every equipped vehicle broadcasts a CAM up to 10 Hz (position, speed, heading, vehicle dimensions). RSUs broadcast DENM hazard alerts. Applications include EEBL, road hazard signalling, road works warning, and slow/stationary vehicle warning. These services operate purely on ITS-G5 direct V2X in the 5.9 GHz band and require no cloud connectivity. 2 Day-1.5 — Infrastructure-assisted and extended services : Builds on Day-1 with more message types (SPATEM/MAPEM for green-light advisory, IVIM for in-vehicle signs) and the hybrid V2I + V2N architecture of C-Roads. Road operators deploy RSUs at priority corridors; vehicles begin receiving traffic management centre data. Security credential management (EU CCMS) is activated for production deployments. 3 Day-2 — Cooperative perception and automated driving support : Introduced conceptually in Release 2. Collective Perception Messages (CPM) let vehicles share sensor detections (detected objects, free-space maps) with each other and with infrastructure. Vulnerable road user Awareness Messages (VAM) protect pedestrians and cyclists. Manoeuvre Coordination Messages (MCM) begin to support cooperative automated driving. Multi-Channel Operation (MCO) / Resource Management at the facilities layer handles the increased channel load. IPv6 integration (Release 2 profile) enables seamless roaming between direct V2X and cellular paths. ● Release ≠ Day "Release" is a standards concept; "Day" is a deployment concept. Day-1 services are covered by Release 1 standards. Day-1.5 and Day-2 services draw on Release 2 standards and, where backwards-compatible, can be deployed alongside Release 1 equipment. ETSI Release 1 vs Release 2 ETSI adopts a release-oriented development process (analogous to 3GPP releases). Each release is a coherent toolbox of standards — functionality specs, sub-system specs, testing specs, and framing documents — from which implementers and profiling bodies (C2C-CC, C-Roads) build deployable systems. A Release x+1 station must be backward-compatible with Release x: it must obtain the same level of service in a Release x environment, and a Release x station must maintain full functionality in a Release x+1 environment (a regulatory requirement for C-ITS per Directive (EU) 2023/2661). sectionTitle: The standards ecosystem — who makes what
text: The standards ecosystem — who makes what C-ITS interoperability is the product of coordinated work across several Standards Developing Organizations (SDOs), industry consortia, and regulatory bodies. No single organisation owns the full stack: 🇪🇺 ETSI TC ITS European Telecommunications Standards Institute, Technical Committee ITS. Produces the normative EN and TS specifications covering the full protocol stack: access layer (ITS-G5, C-V2X), GeoNetworking, BTP, facilities messages (CAM, DENM, CPM, VAM…), security formats, and management. Releases are catalogued in ETSI TR 101 607. 🌐 CEN / ISO CEN TC 278 and ISO TC 204 cover road transport informatics. Key contributions include the DATEX II data exchange standard (used by NAPCORE / NAPs for SRTI), cooperative ITS station specifications harmonised with ETSI, and EFC (Electronic Fee Collection) standards that coexist in the 5.8–5.9 GHz band. 🇺🇸 IEEE / SAE IEEE 802.11p (now folded into IEEE 802.11-2025 including 802.11bd) defines the PHY/MAC underlying ITS-G5. SAE J2735 defines the DSRC message set (BSM, MAP, SPaT) widely deployed in North America. ETSI ITS is harmonised with these where technically feasible. 🛣️ C-Roads Platform EU-funded project bringing together road operators from 20+ member states. Publishes the harmonised C-ITS specifications profile (C-Roads Profile, "Release 2" edition) that maps ETSI toolbox standards to concrete, interoperable deployment requirements. The reference for European road operator rollout. 🏎️ CAR 2 CAR Communication Consortium (C2C-CC) Industry consortium of vehicle manufacturers and suppliers. Publishes the Basic System Profile (BSP) that profiles ETSI standards for OBU implementation. Together with C-Roads, C2C-CC defines the interoperability baseline used in European type approval. ⚖️ EU Commission & Regulation Directive 2010/40/EU (ITS Directive) and its amendment Directive (EU) 2023/2661 set the legal framework and mandate for C-ITS deployment. Delegated Regulations cover SRTI (No 886/2013), RTTI (2015/962), and NAPs (2022/670). The EU CCMS manages the root-of-trust for C-ITS security certificates in Europe.

The protocol stack — a preview Every C-ITS station implements a layered protocol architecture derived from the OSI reference model. The ETSI ITS-S architecture maps onto OSI as follows: the Access Layer covers OSI layers 1 and 2; the Networking & Transport Layer covers OSI layers 3 and 4; the Facilities Layer covers OSI layers 5–7; and Applications sit above the stack. Two cross-cutting planes — Security and Management — interact with all layers. Security Applications CAM, DENM, CPM, VAM, SPATEM, MAPEM, IVIM, MCM … Facilities Layer Message encoding (ASN.1), LDM, PoTi, Service Announcement, Resource Management Networking & Transport GeoNetworking (EN 302 636-4-1) · BTP (EN 302 636-5-1) · IPv6/GN (EN 302 636-6-1) Access Layer ITS-G5 / IEEE 802.11p/bd (EN 302 663) · C-V2X LTE/5G-NR (TS 103 723) · DCC / RM Management The key architectural insight is that C-ITS direct communication is constellation-based rather than configuration-based: no TCP handshake, no session establishment. A vehicle's OBU broadcasts its CAM message into the radio medium; all stations in range receive and decode it autonomously. Security (signing with a pseudonym certificate) happens at the Networking & Transport Layer so that GeoNetworking can forward signed packets without unpacking them. ● Dive deeper The full layer-by-layer breakdown — including protocol field details, timing rules, and message flows — is in the Architecture page. Individual message pages cover CAM , DENM , CPM , VAM , and MCM .

CORE STANDARD ITS Station Architecture Every C-ITS device — whether a car, a roadside unit, a traffic-management centre, or a smartphone — is modelled as an ITS Station (ITS-S). The ITS-S reference architecture, defined in ETSI EN 302 665 (equivalent to ISO 21217), specifies a layered OSI-based protocol stack augmented by two cross-cutting vertical entities — Management and Security — that span all layers. Understanding this architecture is the prerequisite for everything else in C-ITS. ETSI EN 302 665 ISO 21217 ETSI TR 103 902 ETSI TS 103 697 Why a Reference Architecture? Cooperative ITS must work across an enormous range of contexts: a vehicle travelling at motorway speed, a roadside gantry with a fixed backhaul, a traffic-management centre receiving data from thousands of sensors, and a pedestrian with a smartphone. The communication technologies also vary — ITS-G5 (DSRC-derived 5 GHz radio), LTE/5G-NR, infrared, satellite broadcast, and more. Without a common framework, interoperability would be impossible. ETSI EN 302 665 solves this by defining a single ITS Station Reference Architecture that every conformant ITS-S must follow. The architecture is deliberately a tool-box : conformance does not require implementing every element, but every implemented element must follow the defined structure and interfaces. The design follows the OSI layered model extended to include ITS applications above the stack, plus the two cross-cutting entities. ● One architecture, all station types The same ITS-S reference architecture applies to vehicle OBUs, roadside RSUs, central servers, and personal devices. What differs is which functional components are present and how many physical units implement them. The architecture is aligned with the parallel ISO TC204 WG16 CALM (Communications Access for Land Mobiles) work — ISO 21217 covers the same architecture at the international level, while ETSI EN 302 665 is the European transposition. The Four Horizontal Layers The protocol stack in the ITS-S reference architecture has three communication layers, extended upward by an applications block. From bottom to top: Management Applications ITS-S applications — road safety, traffic efficiency, other Facilities OSI layers 5–7 · LDM · encoding · HMI · session support Networking & Transport OSI layers 3–4 · GeoNetworking · IPv6 · BTP · UDP/TCP Access OSI layers 1–2 · ITS-G5 · LTE-V2X · IR · DSRC · PHY + MAC/LLC Security Each layer exposes a Service Access Point (SAP) upward and downward, and also connects to the Management and Security entities through named interfaces (see the Interfaces section below). Access Layer (AL) The Access Layer (AL) covers OSI layers 1 and 2 — the Physical Layer (PHY) and Data Link Layer (DLL). The DLL is subdivided into a Medium Access Control (MAC) sub-layer and a Logical Link Control (LLC) sub-layer. The AL is technology-agnostic in the architecture: the same layer management framework wraps ITS-G5, LTE-V2X, infrared, and legacy DSRC technologies. To accommodate legacy access technologies a Communication Adaptation Layer (CAL) may sit at the top of the DLL, together with a Management Adaptation Entity (MAE) and a Security Adaptation Entity (SAE). The AL provides upward services via the IN-interface to Networking & Transport, connects to Management via the MI-interface, and to Security via the SI-interface. Logical Channels (LCHs) are numbered sequentially (LCH0 to LCH255) and mapped onto physical channels by the access technology standard. LCH0 is reserved for management communications between ITS stations; LCH1 for service advertisement / session initialization; LCH2 for data exchange in sessions. Prioritization operates at two levels: just below the IN-interface (DLL priority queues per-station) and inside the PHY (channel contention classes, e.g. the four IEEE 802.11p access categories AC_VO, AC_VI, AC_BE, AC_BK). See the Access Layer page for full protocol details. Networking & Transport Layer (N&T) The Networking & Transport Layer covers OSI layers 3 and 4. It supports multiple networking protocols simultaneously, including: GeoNetworking (GN) — topology-free geographic addressing and forwarding IPv6 with mobility support (ISO 21210) IPv6 over GeoNetworking (ETSI TS 102 636-6-1) CALM FAST protocol (non-IP single-hop, ISO 29281) Other protocols as needed Transport protocols available include UDP, TCP, and ITS-specific dedicated transport protocols such as BTP (Basic Transport Protocol). Each networking protocol may pair with its own dedicated transport protocol or with a standard one. The layer connects upward to Facilities via the NF-interface, to Access via the IN-interface, to Management via the MN-interface, and to Security via the SN-interface. See the Networking & Transport page for GeoNetworking and BTP details. Facilities Layer (FL) The Facilities Layer covers OSI layers 5, 6, and 7 for ITS. It provides shared infrastructure services to ITS-S applications, removing the need for every application to re-implement common functionality. Key facilities include: Local Dynamic Map (LDM) — a spatially and temporally indexed store of dynamic objects Position and time support (GNSS integration, timestamping) Data presentation — ASN.1 encoding/decoding Addressing support — selection of lower-layer addressing mode Generic HMI support — presenting information to drivers or automated systems Message management — CAMs (periodic), DENMs (event), service messages Relevance checking — whether a received message applies to the current context Station capabilities management — station type, supported channels SOA application protocol support — session establishment, mobility handover Support for DSRC legacy applications Channel selection / CI selection manager The Facilities Layer connects upward to Applications via the FA-interface, downward to Networking & Transport via the NF-interface, to Management via the MF-interface, and to Security via the SF-interface. See the Facilities Layer page for LDM, encoding, and service details. Applications ITS-S applications reside above the Facilities Layer. An ITS application is defined as an association of two or more complementary ITS-S application fragments — for example, a server-side fragment in a central ITS station and a client-side fragment in a vehicle ITS station. Together they provide an ITS service to the user. Applications are initially grouped into: Road Safety, Traffic Efficiency, and Other Applications. Every ITS application must be registered with an ITS application identifier (ITS-AID) and assigned both a priority (which governs the maximum channel access priority at the AL) and a logical channel type for data transmission. See the Applications page for CAM, DENM, CPM, and other services. The Two Vertical Entities: Management and Security Two entities span the entire stack vertically, interfacing with every layer. This makes them cross-layer by definition, which is why they appear as side rails rather than horizontal layers. Management Entity The Communication and Station Management Entity (often called simply the Management entity) is responsible for managing all aspects of communications within the ITS station. It maintains a Management Information Base (MIB) and provides: Cross-interface management Inter-Unit Management Communication (IUMC) Networking management Communications service management ITS application management (install, update, remove) Station management (identity, capabilities) General congestion control coordination ITS service advertisement management (FAST) CI / ITS-S application mapping Local Node Map maintenance Regulatory information management Interfaces: MA (to Applications), MF (to Facilities), MN (to Networking & Transport), MI (to Access), MS (to Security). Security Entity The Security Entity provides security services to all layers and to the Management entity. It maintains a Security Information Base (SIB) and may include Hardware Security Modules (HSMs). Functions include: Firewall and intrusion management Authentication and authorisation Identity, crypto key and certificate management Security profile management Hardware Security Module (HSM) support Interfaces: SA (to Applications), SF (to Facilities), SN (to Networking & Transport), SI (to Access), MS (to Management). ● Security as a sub-entity of Management EN 302 665 notes that Security "can also be considered as a specific part of the management entity." In practice, the two are always shown as distinct entities because their SAP interfaces are specified independently, and an implementation may separate them physically (e.g. a dedicated HSM chip). See the Management page for congestion control, service advertisement, and MIB details. See the Security page for PKI, certificates, and the CCMS. Named Inter-Layer Interfaces (SAPs) The connections between architectural blocks are formally named interfaces. These names appear throughout all ETSI ITS standards and must be understood to read any specification correctly. The naming convention encodes the two entities being connected: the first letter(s) are an entity abbreviation, the second letter is another entity abbreviation. E.g. MN = Management to Networking&Transport; SN = Security to Networking&Transport. sectionTitle: Types of ITS Stations and Sub-systems
text: Types of ITS Stations and Sub-systems Four ITS sub-systems are defined, each containing an ITS station of the corresponding type. The same reference architecture applies to all; what changes is the deployment context and the functional components that are present. 🚗 Vehicle ITS Station Deployed in cars, trucks, motorcycles, and other road vehicles — whether in motion or parked. The vehicle ITS-S typically includes: An ITS-S host (full stack + applications) A vehicle ITS-S gateway — bridges the proprietary in-vehicle network (ECU / CAN bus) to the ITS station-internal network An ITS-S router — connects to ITS ad hoc networks (V2V, V2I via ITS-G5) Access to ECUs is out of scope for EN 302 665; it is implementation-specific. 🚦 Roadside ITS Station Fixed installations on gantries, poles, and at intersections. Roadside ITS-Ss typically have: An ITS-S host A roadside ITS-S gateway — bridges sensors (inductive loops, variable message signs) to the ITS station-internal network An ITS-S router — ITS ad hoc (V2I / I2V) An ITS-S border router — connects to core networks / Internet 🏢 Central ITS Station Traffic-management centres, cloud back-ends, and map providers. Central ITS-Ss typically include: An ITS-S host A central ITS-S gateway — bridges the central system to the ITS station-internal network An ITS-S border router — connects to infrastructure / Internet 📱 Personal ITS Station Hand-held devices such as smartphones, PDAs, or wearables carried by pedestrians or cyclists (Vulnerable Road Users). A personal ITS-S: Contains the full ITS-S host May also perform HMI functionality for another ITS sub-system, connecting via the ITS station-internal network Sends VAM (VRU Awareness Messages) to warn nearby vehicles ● ITS station-internal network When a single ITS station is implemented across multiple physical units (e.g. a separate OBU and antenna unit in a vehicle), they are interconnected via the ITS station-internal network . This internal network may be wired (Ethernet) or wireless (Bluetooth). From a protocol perspective there is no difference between an internal and an external communication interface — the same management and security frameworks apply.

sectionTitle: Functional Components within an ITS Station
text: Functional Components within an ITS Station Within a single ITS-S sub-system, different functional components may be present. These define the functional role and protocol depth of each unit: ITS-S Host Implements the full ITS station reference architecture including ITS-S applications. This is the minimal entity that can originate or terminate ITS application data. Every ITS station contains at least one ITS-S host. ITS-S Router Implements all layers of the reference architecture except Applications and Facilities. Interconnects two different ITS protocol stacks at layer 3 (networking layer). May convert protocols. Typically connects the ITS station-internal network to an ITS ad hoc network. ITS-S Border Router Same function as an ITS-S router but the external protocol stack may not follow ITS management and security principles. Used to connect the ITS domain to the generic domain (e.g. Internet, cellular). One side is the ITS stack; the other side is a generic OSI stack (layers 1–3). ITS-S Gateway Interconnects two different OSI protocol stacks at layers 5–7. Converts protocols between the proprietary network (e.g. CAN bus with ECUs, roadside sensor networks) and the ITS station-internal network. Used in vehicle, roadside, and central sub-systems. ITS-S Interceptor Generic term covering ITS-S gateway, ITS-S router, ITS-S border router, or any implementation-specific connector between the ITS station-internal network and another network. ITS ad hoc network ITS-S Router Core / Internet ITS-S Border Router Proprietary Network (ECU/sensors) ITS-S Gateway ITS Station-Internal Network ITS-S host(s) · ITS-S routers · ITS-S gateways · ITS-S border routers Networking view: an ITS station connects to ITS ad hoc networks via ITS-S routers, to access/core networks via ITS-S border routers, and to proprietary local networks via ITS-S gateways.

ITS Domain vs. Generic Domain ITSC distinguishes two domains: ITS Domain All elements of ITSC specified in ITS/ITSC standards. Corresponds to what ISO TC204 WG16 calls "CALM-aware." The full reference architecture with Management and Security entities applies within this domain. Generic Domain Legacy or non-ITS elements used for ITSC — e.g. the public Internet, a cellular network, a CAN bus. Corresponds to "Non-CALM-aware" in CALM terminology. ITS-S border routers sit at the boundary between the two domains. The ITS-S border router exists specifically to bridge these two domains. On the ITS side it implements the full ITS management and security framework; on the generic side it speaks standard OSI layers 1–3 without the ITS-specific overhead. ● Management and security do not cross the border router The ITS management entity and security entity apply only within the ITS domain. On the far side of an ITS-S border router, standard network security mechanisms (TLS, IPsec, etc.) must be used instead. This boundary is critical to understand when designing V2N (Vehicle-to-Network) deployments.

Release 2 Architecture Evolution The original EN 302 665 (Release 1, 2010) defined the single-channel baseline. ETSI ITS Release 2, driven by the need to support a much larger number of use cases and messages simultaneously, introduced significant architectural additions. Key Release 2 principles, as collected in ETSI TR 103 902: R1 Single-channel One channel, limited use cases; Release 1 baseline R2 Multi-channel Multiple simultaneous channels via MCO architecture BCK Backward compatible R2 stations interoperate with R1 in mixed deployments Backward Compatibility Requirements A Release 2 ITS-S must be able to provide the same level of service as a Release 1 station when operating in a Release 1 environment (REQ_APP_001 to REQ_APP_003 in TS 103 697). Release 2 applications that use a channel configuration shared with Release 1 must ensure backward compatibility. Release-specific applications must not interfere with Release 1 applications running on the same channel. New Terminology in Release 2 (TR 103 902) Term Definition C-ITS Ecosystem Cooperative ITS specific ecosystem — the totality of standards, regulations, and stakeholders C-ITS-S Cooperative ITS Station — an ITS-S that is part of the C-ITS ecosystem and its trust model ITS Constellation (ITS-C) Group of ITS-Ss actively exchanging information Direct V2X (Short V2X) Localized V2X without intermediary IP networks, base-stations, or Internet routing Indirect V2X V2X using IP-based protocols over cellular/fixed-line networks Networked V2X (V2N2X) Data sourcing ITS-S provides data to intermediary networks which transfer it to sinking ITS-Ss ALI (Access Layer Instance) A fully parameterised (service channel, technology, TX power) transceiver entity Backward compatibility Rx+1 station provides same service level as Rx station in Rx environment Selected Release 2 terms from ETSI TR 103 902

Multi-Channel Operation (MCO) Architecture Multi-Channel Operation (MCO) is the key Release 2 architectural addition defined in ETSI TS 103 697 . In Release 1, a single channel is used and applications statically share it. In Release 2, multiple channels (and multiple access technologies) operate simultaneously, requiring a coordinating mechanism to allocate bandwidth fairly among competing applications. ● MCO is a cross-layer functionality MCO sub-functionalities exist at three layers simultaneously — Facilities (MCO_FAC), Networking & Transport (MCO_NET), and Access (MCO_ACC) — making it a true cross-layer architecture element. Management Plane Applications Message Triggering Entities (MTEs) · provide Functional Configuration Profiles (FCPs) Facilities — MCO_FAC BME · MHE · MCE · Bandwidth management · channel selection decisions Networking & Transport — MCO_NET GN Core · ALI Group Handlers (GAGHs) · MPU · NU · ARH Access — MCO_ACC ALI Operations · TRX info Collection · multiple simultaneous transceivers Data Plane MCO Entities at the Facilities Layer (MCO_FAC) Bandwidth Management Entity (BME) Collects application requirements and lower-layer capabilities; sends feedback to applications to adapt their transmission rate; configures lower layers to use the most adequate channel/technology combination. Message Handling Entity (MHE) Transmits messages toward the Networking & Transport layer; configures per-message parameters considering available radio interfaces and channels. Decides which Access Layer Instance (ALI) to use per message. Message Collecting Entity (MCE) Collects received messages from the Networking & Transport layer and forwards them to the appropriate Message Receiving Entity (MRE) at the Facilities layer. MCO Mechanisms 1. Functional Configuration Profiles (FCPs) Each application characterises its communication needs as a Functional Configuration Profile (FCP), identified by a unique FcpID. FCPs may specify primary and secondary channels, priority, and other parameters. In Release 1, dissemination configurations are statically defined (e.g. CAS always uses one fixed channel; if congested, CAMs are simply dropped). In Release 2, the BME evaluates all active FCPs and returns Functional Configuration Limits (FCLs) — telling each application what the actual allowed configuration is given current network conditions and competing applications. The FcpID is then passed per-message at the data plane so the MHE can apply the correct configuration. 2. Access Layer Instances (ALIs) An Access Layer Instance (ALI) is a fully parameterised instantiation of a transceiver — combining access technology (e.g. ITS-G5 or LTE-V2X), service channel, TX power, and other parameters into a single identifier (AliID). Groups of ALIs using the same service channel and technology form ALI Groups (identified by AliGroupID). The MHE selects the AliID per message and passes it downward via the NL-PDU header. This allows the Access layer to route each frame to the correct transceiver with the correct parameters without higher-layer involvement. A-PDU Application Data Unit FL-PDU Facilities Header (FH) added NL-PDU Transport + Network Headers (TH/NH) added AL-PDU Access Header (AH) added — transmitted frame MCO data flow: headers are added at each layer as data moves downward. A-PDU + FH = FL-PDU; FL-PDU + TH/NH = NL-PDU; NL-PDU + AH = AL-PDU (transmitted frame). MCO Application Requirements (TS 103 697, Clause 7) Req. Decentralized Congestion Control (DCC) Decentralized Congestion Control (DCC) is the mechanism that prevents any single ITS station from consuming all available channel capacity. In a dense vehicular network — hundreds of vehicles near an accident — channel congestion causes safety messages to be lost exactly when they matter most. DCC ensures graceful degradation: as the channel fills up, each station reduces its own contributions proportionally, preserving fairness and leaving headroom for emergency traffic. ● DCC is Cross-Layer by Design DCC is not a single protocol but a distributed control framework spanning the access layer (DCC_ACC), the networking & transport layer (DCC_NET), the facilities layer (DCC_FAC), and coordinated by a cross-layer management entity (DCC_CROSS). This is necessary because the access layer alone cannot know which applications are running — application priorities must feed back down to restrict less-important traffic first while preserving safety-critical flows. Channel Busy Ratio (CBR) The primary congestion metric is the Channel Busy Ratio (CBR) : the fraction of time during the last 100 ms measurement window (T_CBR = 100 ms) that the receiver perceived the channel as busy. A channel is considered busy when a received ITS-G5 signal exceeds −85 dBm . Formally: CBR = T_busy / T_CBR. The busy time T_busy is accumulated in milliseconds over 100 ms. Any equivalent mechanism providing CBR within ±3% deviation is acceptable (EN 302 663 §4.3.2). In Release 2 (EN 303 797), the notation is sharpened: LCBR (Local CBR — measured by this station) vs GCBR (Global CBR — derived from neighbouring stations' reported LCBR, e.g. via GeoNetworking headers). When GCBR is available it supersedes LCBR as the DCC input, giving a wider view of congestion around the ego station. Hard Regulatory Limits (EN 302 571 / EN 303 797) Absolute limits that all DCC algorithms must respect, regardless of internal logic: Ton ≤ 4 ms — maximum duration of a single transmission burst. Duty cycle ≤ 3 % per second per channel (δ_max = 0.03). Toff ≥ 25 ms — minimum gap between consecutive transmissions. When CBR ≥ CTH (default congestion threshold CTH = 0.62 for the CCH / 5895–5905 MHz channel): Toff ≥ min(1 000 ms, Ton × (4 000 × CBR/(1 − CBR) − 1)). ● Toff Calculation Example Suppose Ton = 1 ms and CBR = 0.70. The congestion threshold CTH = 0.62 is exceeded. Toff_limit = 1 × (4 000 × 0.70/0.30 − 1) ≈ 9 332 ms. Capped at 1 000 ms, so the station must wait 1 second between messages — effectively throttled to 1 Hz regardless of application demands. Two Conformant DCC Algorithm Families TS 102 687 DCC Access Layer specifies two algorithm families; implementations must choose one: Reactive DCC A finite state machine evaluated every T_CBR (100 ms). States are ordered linearly: Relaxed → Active 1 → Active 2 → Active 3 → Restrictive . Only transitions to adjacent states are allowed (one step per 100 ms cycle — a form of hysteresis). Each state defines the allowed packet rate and minimum Toff. Adaptive DCC (LIMERIC-inspired) A linear control algorithm running every 200 ms. Computes a target duty cycle δ aiming for CBR_target = 0.68. Control parameters: α = 0.016 (smoothing), β = 0.0012 (gain), G⁺_max = 0.0005, G⁻_max = −0.00025. Bounds: δ_max = 0.03, δ_min = 0.0006. A gate keeper enforces δ by delaying packet acceptance. Reactive DCC State Machine Relaxed CBR < 30 % 10 Hz Toff 100 ms ↔ Active 1 30–39 % 5 Hz Toff 200 ms ↔ Active 2 40–49 % 2.5 Hz Toff 400 ms ↔ Active 3 50–60 % 2 Hz Toff 500 ms ↔ Restrictive CBR > 60 % 1 Hz Toff 1 000 ms Bidirectional arrows indicate only adjacent transitions are permitted. One step per 100 ms T_CBR evaluation cycle. Reactive DCC states — transitions only between neighbours. Example Toff/rate for Ton < 1 ms (TS 102 687 Annex A). DCC Control Knobs: TPC, TRC, TDC TPC — Transmit Power Control Reduce output power to shrink the interference footprint. Stations further away experience less signal, so their CBR measurement drops. Used as a first-line defence to limit reach before cutting message rate. TRC — Transmit Rate Control Increase Toff (the inter-packet gap). Fewer packets per second means less airtime consumed by the ego station. The primary mechanism used by both reactive and adaptive DCC. TDC — Transmit Datarate Control Switch to a higher MCS (e.g. 24 Mbit/s instead of 6 Mbit/s). Shorter Ton for the same payload means less airtime per packet. Only useful when link quality allows higher modulation without reliability degradation. Cross-Layer DCC Architecture TS 103 175 Cross-Layer DCC specifies how DCC entities at different layers collaborate via the management plane (DCC_CROSS entity): DCC_CROSS (Management plane): evaluates all inputs, distributes Toff limits and power limits downward DCC_FAC — Facilities Layer Receives message-generation rate limits from management; sheds lower-priority CAM/DENM generation first under congestion DCC_NET — Networking & Transport Channel routing — selects CCH vs SCH based on congestion state; embeds local CBR in GeoNetworking headers for sharing DCC_ACC — Access Layer Gate keeper: enforces Ton/Toff limits; measures local CBR every 100 ms; controls TX power and MCS per packet ● DCC Profile Identifiers (DP0–DP32) TS 102 724 introduces DCC Profile Identifiers (DP-ID) that classify traffic streams. DP1/DP2 map to CCH safety traffic (CAM, DENM), DP3–DP8 to CCH non-safety, DP9–DP13+ to SCH-specific services. Each profile carries its own Toff requirement per DCC state and its own channel assignment priority. This lets the management entity shed non-safety traffic first while preserving DP1/DP2 safety traffic even in Restrictive state.

sectionTitle: Coexistence with CEN DSRC Road Tolling
text: Coexistence with CEN DSRC Road Tolling Road tolling in Europe uses CEN DSRC (Dedicated Short-Range Communication), standardised in CEN EN 12253 and operating in the 5 795–5 815 MHz band. This band lies just below the ITS-G5B sub-band. Studies (ECC Reports 101 and 228, ETSI TR 102 654) confirmed that ITS transmissions can interfere with DSRC toll-readers when vehicles pass through charging portals. TS 102 792 CEN DSRC Mitigation specifies mandatory mitigation for all ITS stations in ITS-G5A/B/D: 1 Protected Zone Database: Each ITS station holds a database of DSRC installation positions (toll plazas, tunnel entries, parking gates) with associated GPS coordinates and protected zone radii. The database may be pre-loaded statically, or dynamically updated from roadside ITS stations broadcasting their position and protected zone radius in CAMs. 2 Normal Mode (outside zones): ITS station operates with default parameters — up to 23 dBm EIRP. Unwanted emissions in the 5 795–5 815 MHz tolling band must not exceed −33 dBm/MHz EIRP. 3 Coexistence Mode (inside protected zone): When an ITS station enters a protected zone, it switches to coexistence mode. Output power and duty cycle are severely restricted. For LTE-V2X stations (EN 303 613 §5.7.3), maximum power inside a protected zone is 10 dBm EIRP and spurious emissions in the tolling band are capped at −65 dBm/MHz. 4 Duty Cycle Restriction: Inside the zone the allowed transmit duty cycle drops dramatically. The Toff between messages grows to keep aggregate interference below the field strength threshold where DSRC reliability is impaired. Calculations in TS 102 792 Annex A show that Toff grows roughly linearly with the number of ITS interferers. Both ITS-G5 (EN 302 663 §4.4, EN 303 797 §4.7) and LTE-V2X (EN 303 613 §5.7.3) require conformance to TS 102 792. Fixed ITS stations near toll plazas have simplified rules since their position is known.

C-V2X / LTE-V2X Access Layer (PC5 Sidelink) LTE-V2X (Long Term Evolution based Vehicle-to-Everything), standardised in 3GPP Release 14, uses the PC5 sidelink interface for direct V2X communication without base-station involvement (Mode 4: autonomous resource selection). ETSI profiles the ITS-specific configuration in EN 303 613 LTE-V2X Access Layer . Protocol Stack Management (MI-SAP) PDCP — Packet Data Convergence Protocol Differentiates IP and Non-IP SDUs (e.g. GeoNetworking encapsulation) RLC — Radio Link Control Segmentation and concatenation of SDUs for MAC transport RRC — Radio Resource Control Access stratum management; configures Mode 4 resource pool parameters NAS — Non-Access Stratum Subscription control and CN requests (mostly bypassed in standalone Mode 4) MAC — Medium Access Control Autonomous resource pool management and scheduling; sensing-based collision avoidance PHY — Physical Layer SC-FDMA / OFDM; PSCCH (control) + PSSCH (data); Band 47 (5 855–5 925 MHz) PC5 Physical Layer Basics Unlike ITS-G5's OFDM with 52 subcarriers at 10 MHz, LTE-V2X PHY uses SC-FDMA / OFDM with a 15 kHz subcarrier spacing in Band 47. Resources are organised into Resource Blocks (RBs — 7 consecutive symbols × 12 consecutive subcarriers in frequency) and sub-channels (contiguous RB sets). The Physical Sidelink Control CHannel (PSCCH) carries scheduling grants; the Physical Sidelink Shared CHannel (PSSCH) carries the actual data payload. In Mode 4, each vehicle autonomously selects resources from a pre-configured resource pool based on sensing: it measures Sidelink RSSI (S-RSSI) over each sub-channel for a configurable sensing window, excludes busy sub-channels, and selects semi-persistent resources from the remainder. C-V2X Congestion Control TS 103 574 C-V2X Congestion Control defines congestion control for the PC5 interface. The key metric is the Channel Busy Ratio (CBR) , which for LTE-V2X is defined as the portion of sub-channels in the resource pool whose S-RSSI exceeds a configured threshold, measured over the last 100 ms. Note this definition differs from the ITS-G5 CBR (energy detect on a 10 MHz channel vs sub-channel RSSI occupancy). Each station adapts its Channel Occupancy Ratio (CR) — the fraction of configured sub-channels it actually uses — so as not to exceed a per-CBR CR limit. Higher CBR forces lower CR: the station must back off by using fewer sub-channels per unit time, reducing its contribution to congestion. ● Mode 4 Resource Reselection Semi-persistent scheduling means a station picks resources valid for multiple consecutive subframes. When the reselection counter reaches zero, the station re-senses and re-selects. This reduces signalling overhead but introduces an inherent collision probability if two stations independently choose the same resources — mitigated by the randomised reselection probability (typically 20 %) and sensing-based exclusion.

Release 2: Multi-Channel Operation and NGV Release 2 of the ETSI ITS standards introduces significant access layer enhancements for both ITS-G5 and C-V2X. The primary Release 2 ITS-G5 access layer document is EN 303 797 ITS-G5 R2 (2024). Multi-Channel Operation (MCO) ETSI TS 103 695 specifies Multi-Channel Operation. ITS stations may carry multiple transceivers, each tuned to a different channel simultaneously, eliminating the old time-sharing constraint. MCO is coordinated by the management plane, which sets channel selection and DCC thresholds per channel — including CTH values that may differ from the default 0.62 when MCO settings are active. Profile 2: IEEE 802.11bd (NGV) IEEE 802.11bd-2022 (Next Generation V2X) adds BPSK-DCM for extended range, 256-QAM for throughput at good link quality, optional 20 MHz channel bonding (max 30 dBm EIRP), midamble insertion for mobility compensation in long packets, and MIMO support. Profile 1 (802.11-2020 legacy mode) remains mandatory; Profile 2 is optional. Global CBR Feedback EN 303 797 formalises LCBR / GCBR distinction. When higher layers provide GCBR — e.g. from GeoNetworking cooperative awareness or dedicated management messages — the access layer substitutes it for LCBR as the DCC input. This improves accuracy at congestion cluster boundaries. C-V2X R2 Congestion TS 103 574 V2.0.0 (2023) establishes the Release 2 baseline for C-V2X PC5 congestion control, referencing V1.1.1 (2018) as the normative foundation. The R2 framework enables future enhancements: multi-channel coordination, global CBR exchange, and improved resource pool definitions aligned with NR-V2X (5G NR PC5).

sectionTitle: Position in the ITS Station Architecture
text: Position in the ITS Station Architecture The access layer occupies the bottom of the ITS station reference architecture (ETSI EN 302 665). It exports a single data interface (IN-SAP) upward and a management interface (MI-SAP) to the management entity. Higher layers see one uniform access interface regardless of whether the underlying radio is ITS-G5 or C-V2X — the key to technology-neutral upper-layer operation. Management (DCC_CROSS, channel config) Applications Road safety, traffic efficiency, infotainment Facilities CAM, DENM, CPM, VAM — message generation; DCC_FAC Networking & Transport GeoNetworking, BTP; DCC_NET — see Networking page Access Layer ITS-G5 (802.11p OCB) or C-V2X (PC5) — this page; DCC_ACC Security (PKI, certificates) The AL_DATA.request primitive carries: source/destination MAC, priority, transmit power, MCS, channel number, transceiver ID, and payload down to the radio. AL_DATA.indication delivers: source/destination MAC, current local CBR, channel number, RSSI, and payload back up to the networking layer. This clean interface decouples radio technology from upper-layer protocol logic. Related pages: Networking & Transport describes GeoNetworking above this layer. Architecture covers the full ITS station reference model. Management covers the management plane including DCC_CROSS.

Networking & Transport GeoNetworking & BTP GeoNetworking is the network-layer protocol at the heart of C-ITS. Unlike IP — which routes packets to a named address — GeoNetworking routes packets to a geographic position or area. This makes it uniquely suited to vehicular ad hoc networks (VANETs), where vehicles move continuously, network topology changes in milliseconds, and many safety messages only matter to vehicles in a specific location. On top of GeoNetworking sits the Basic Transport Protocol (BTP), a four-byte lightweight transport that multiplexes CAM, DENM, and other facility messages to well-known ports — and optionally IPv6 can be carried as well via the GN6ASL adaptation sub-layer. ETSI EN 302 636-1 ETSI EN 302 636-3 ETSI EN 302 636-4-1 ETSI EN 302 636-5-1 ETSI EN 302 636-6-1 ETSI TS 103 836-4-1 ETSI TS 103 836-5-1 Why position-based routing? Classical IP routing maintains tables that map a destination name (address) to a next-hop router. In a VANET this breaks down: a vehicle moving at 130 km/h changes its one-hop neighbours every few seconds, making topology maintenance prohibitively expensive. GeoNetworking sidesteps the problem entirely by routing toward a geographic destination — a coordinate or a shaped area — using the position information that every node already broadcasts in its beacons. No routing-table setup is needed; forwarding decisions are made autonomously, hop by hop, purely from the position information carried in each packet. ● Core insight GeoNetworking provides two coupled functions: geographic addressing (identify the destination by position or area) and geographic forwarding (route each packet toward that position using a partial view of the local network topology). Packets are forwarded "on the fly" without prior signalling. This design meets the hard requirements of vehicular safety: Zero setup latency — no handshake or route discovery before the first packet can be sent. Topology independence — works in sparse and dense networks, with or without roadside infrastructure. Area targeting — a vehicle can send a hazard warning exactly to the circle or rectangle ahead where other vehicles are affected, without flooding the whole network. Multi-hop — intermediate vehicles relay packets, extending range well beyond a single radio hop. GeoNetworking is specified across a family of ETSI standards. Release 1 is the EN 302 636 series. Release 2 supersedes it with the TS 103 836 series (see the R1 vs R2 section below). Both releases share the same fundamental packet format; they are wire-compatible. It sits above the Access Layer (ITS-G5 / C-V2X) and below the Facilities Layer (CAM, DENM, …). The media-independent part defines all packet formats, forwarding algorithms, and data structures. GeoNetworking packet header structure Every GeoNetworking packet begins with a fixed-size Basic Header (4 bytes), followed by a fixed-size Common Header (8 bytes), and then an optional Extended Header whose size and content depend on the packet transport type (GUC, GBC, SHB, etc.). Non-linear encoding: 6-bit Multiplier x Base (50 ms / 1 s / 10 s / 100 s). Range: 0 ms to 6 300 s RHL (Remaining Hop Limit) 8 bit Decremented by 1 at each forwarding node. Packet is dropped when RHL reaches 0 Fields of the GeoNetworking Basic Header (4 octets total) Common Header fields Field Size Description NH (Next Header) 4 bit Upper-layer protocol: 0=ANY, 1=BTP-A, 2=BTP-B, 3=IPv6 Reserved 4 bit Set to 0 HT (Header Type) 4 bit Packet type: 1=BEACON, 2=GUC, 3=GAC, 4=GBC, 5=TSB, 6=LS HST (Header Sub-Type) 4 bit Sub-type, e.g. area shape: 0=CIRCLE, 1=RECT, 2=ELIP; or for TSB: 0=SHB, 1=multi-hop TC (Traffic Class) 8 bit SCF bit (store-carry-forward), Channel Offload bit, 6-bit TC ID mapped to EDCA queues Flags 8 bit Bit 0: IS_MOBILE (1=vehicle, 0=stationary); bits 1 to 7 reserved PL (Payload Length) 16 bit Length in octets of everything following the complete GeoNetworking header (BTP + message) MHL (Max Hop Limit) 8 bit Hop limit set by the source; not decremented during forwarding (carried for informational use) Reserved 8 bit Set to 0 Fields of the GeoNetworking Common Header (8 octets total) ● LT vs RHL LT (Lifetime) limits how long a packet may be buffered while waiting for a suitable next hop — relevant in store-carry-forward scenarios. RHL (Remaining Hop Limit) limits the number of wireless hops the packet may traverse. Both work together to bound packet propagation in time and space. Position Vectors GeoNetworking uses two position vector formats embedded in the Extended Header: Long Position Vector (LPV) — 24 bytes GN_ADDR (8 B) + TST timestamp in TAI milliseconds since 2004-01-01 (4 B) + Latitude in 1/10 micro-degree (4 B) + Longitude (4 B) + PAI accuracy indicator (1 bit) + Speed in 0.01 m/s (15 bits signed) + Heading in 0.1 degree (16 bits). Used in the Source Position Vector (SO PV) field of most extended headers. Short Position Vector (SPV) — 20 bytes GN_ADDR (8 B) + TST (4 B) + Latitude (4 B) + Longitude (4 B). Omits speed and heading to save bytes. Used in the Destination Position Vector (DE PV) of GUC and in Location Service packets. GeoNetworking address format Every GeoAdhoc router has a unique GeoNetworking address (GN_ADDR) — 8 bytes wide, structured as: M bit (1=manually configured / 0=auto) + ST field (5-bit ITS-S type: 0=Unknown, 1=Pedestrian, 2=Cyclist, 5=Passenger Car, 6=Bus, 15=RSU, …) + 10 reserved bits + MID (48-bit MAC-layer address). The MID maps directly to the link-layer address, enabling GN6ASL to present a virtual Ethernet interface to IPv6. Packet transport types GeoNetworking defines several packet transport types, selected by the HT/HST fields in the Common Header. Each type has distinct forwarding semantics, a different Extended Header structure, and is used for different application scenarios. Type HT/HST Scope Re-broadcast? Typical use GUC GeoUnicast 2 / 0 Point-to-point to a specific GN_ADDR / position No (unicast) Location service reply, unicast data to known destination GBC GeoBroadcast 4 / 0–2 All nodes inside a geographic area (circle, rect, ellipse) Yes (inside area) DENM hazard warning to affected zone, MAPEM/SPATEM GAC GeoAnycast 3 / 0–2 Any one node inside a geographic area No (stops at first receiver) Query to nearest RSU SHB Single-Hop Broadcast 5 / 0 All direct neighbours (1 hop only) No CAM cooperative awareness (primary use case) TSB Topo-Scoped Broadcast 5 / 1 All nodes within N hops Yes (up to MHL) Emergency warnings to N-hop neighbourhood BEACON 1 / 0 All direct neighbours (no payload) No Neighbour discovery when no other traffic is present GeoNetworking packet transport types (EN 302 636-4-1, table 9) ● SHB vs CAM CAM messages are by far the most frequent GeoNetworking traffic. They are always sent as SHB (Single-Hop Broadcast) — no forwarding, no duplication, no area — just "here I am" to every vehicle in direct radio range. This design minimises channel load: each CAM is transmitted exactly once at the source and heard by neighbours directly. Multi-hop propagation is not needed because CAMs are re-generated independently by every vehicle. Geographical areas GBC, GAC, and the GUC destination position all reference geographic locations. The standard (referencing ETSI EN 302 931) defines three area shapes for GBC/GAC, each encoded in the Extended Header: Circle Defined by centre (latitude, longitude) and radius in metres. Simple and adequate for omnidirectional events such as a stationary hazard or a road-works zone. HST=0. Rectangle Defined by centre, two semi-axis lengths (distance A along the heading, distance B perpendicular) and an orientation angle. Suited to a stretch of road or a highway corridor. HST=1. Ellipse Same parameterisation as rectangle but with an elliptical boundary. Provides a smooth boundary modelling irregular coverage areas. HST=2. Forwarding algorithms & the Location Table When a GeoAdhoc router receives a packet that needs to be forwarded, it consults its Location Table (LocT) to determine the best next-hop. Two main categories of forwarding algorithm are defined: Non-area forwarding (GeoUnicast) Greedy Forwarding (GF) Select the neighbour from the Location Table that is geographically closest to the destination (Most Forward within Radius, MFR criterion). Fast and simple — works well in dense networks. May fail when no closer neighbour exists ("local maximum" / void region). Contention-Based Forwarding (CBF) Instead of the source selecting a next hop, every potential forwarder independently decides whether to forward. Each node sets a timer inversely proportional to its distance progress toward the destination; the closest node forwards first and its transmission suppresses the others. Reduces the need for accurate neighbour position knowledge at the sender. Area forwarding (GBC/GAC) Simple GeoBroadcast Flood inside the destination area: every node inside the area rebroadcasts the packet once (after checking the Duplicate Packet List). Robust but potentially high channel load. Area CBF (Contention-Based Forwarding) Timer-based self-selection applied inside the destination area. Nodes outside the area use greedy forwarding to carry the packet toward the area boundary. Suppresses redundant retransmissions. Area Advanced Forwarding Combines greedy forwarding toward the area boundary with CBF inside, plus an additional suppression mechanism using the sender position vector. Defined in Annex

The standard (referencing ETSI EN 302 931) defines three area shapes for GBC/GAC, each encoded in the Extended Header: Circle Defined by centre (latitude, longitude) and radius in metres. Simple and adequate for omnidirectional events such as a stationary hazard or a road-works zone. HST=0. Rectangle Defined by centre, two semi-axis lengths (distance A along the heading, distance B perpendicular) and an orientation angle. Suited to a stretch of road or a highway corridor. HST=1. Ellipse Same parameterisation as rectangle but with an elliptical boundary. Provides a smooth boundary modelling irregular coverage areas. HST=2.

Forwarding algorithms & the Location Table When a GeoAdhoc router receives a packet that needs to be forwarded, it consults its Location Table (LocT) to determine the best next-hop. Two main categories of forwarding algorithm are defined: Non-area forwarding (GeoUnicast) Greedy Forwarding (GF) Select the neighbour from the Location Table that is geographically closest to the destination (Most Forward within Radius, MFR criterion). Fast and simple — works well in dense networks. May fail when no closer neighbour exists ("local maximum" / void region). Contention-Based Forwarding (CBF) Instead of the source selecting a next hop, every potential forwarder independently decides whether to forward. Each node sets a timer inversely proportional to its distance progress toward the destination; the closest node forwards first and its transmission suppresses the others. Reduces the need for accurate neighbour position knowledge at the sender. Area forwarding (GBC/GAC) Simple GeoBroadcast Flood inside the destination area: every node inside the area rebroadcasts the packet once (after checking the Duplicate Packet List). Robust but potentially high channel load. Area CBF (Contention-Based Forwarding) Timer-based self-selection applied inside the destination area. Nodes outside the area use greedy forwarding to carry the packet toward the area boundary. Suppresses redundant retransmissions. Area Advanced Forwarding Combines greedy forwarding toward the area boundary with CBF inside, plus an additional suppression mechanism using the sender position vector. Defined in Annex F of EN 302 636-4-1. ● Forwarding a DENM to a road zone Source vehicle creates a GBC packet with a rectangular area covering 500 m ahead on the highway. Neighbours outside the area receive it and apply greedy forwarding — each relays it toward the area using the closest-to-area neighbour from their LocT. Once a node is inside the area it rebroadcasts using area CBF — it starts a timer; if it hears another node broadcast first (from a better position), it cancels its own transmission. Every vehicle in the zone receives the DENM and delivers it upward to the DENM facility. Location Table (LocT) The Location Table is the central data structure for forwarding decisions. Every GeoAdhoc router maintains one LocT, with one entry per known neighbour or recently heard station. Each Location Table Entry (LocTE) holds: GN_ADDR and LL_ADDR (link-layer address) ITS-S type and GeoNetworking protocol version Long Position Vector (position, speed, heading, timestamp, accuracy indicator PAI) IS_NEIGHBOUR flag (direct radio range) and LS_PENDING flag (Location Service in progress) Duplicate Packet List (DPL) for duplicate detection Packet data rate PDR(GN_ADDR) as Exponential Moving Average (EMA) — used by DCC Entries are soft-state : each has a lifetime (itsGnLifetimeLocTE). If not refreshed by a new beacon or received packet, the entry is deleted. This ensures stale position data does not mislead the forwarding algorithm. ● Location Service (LS) If a GeoUnicast packet must be sent to a destination whose position is not in the LocT, GeoNetworking invokes the Location Service : an LS Request is broadcast (TSB) to find the destination; the destination replies with an LS Reply (GUC) containing its Long Position Vector. While LS is pending, outbound packets for that destination are buffered in the LS packet buffer . After the LS completes, buffered packets are flushed in FIFO order.

DCC interaction GeoNetworking is tightly coupled with Decentralised Congestion Control (DCC) . The ITS-G5 channel at 5.9 GHz has limited bandwidth; when too many vehicles transmit simultaneously, reliability drops. DCC (specified in ETSI TS 102 687 / TS 103 175) monitors channel load and instructs GeoNetworking to: Reduce packet transmission rates (Transmit Rate Control, TRC) Reduce transmission power (Transmit Power Control, TPC) Limit packet data rate per source — the LocT's PDR field tracks each station's per-source packet rate as an EMA, enabling DCC rate enforcement at the network layer Restrict geographical area size for GBC packets (Annex B of EN 302 636-4-1) The TC (Traffic Class) field in the Common Header encodes three sub-fields: the SCF (store-carry-forward) bit, the Channel Offload bit, and a 6-bit TC ID. SCF=1 means the packet may be buffered when no neighbour exists; SCF=0 requires immediate discard. The TC ID maps to media-dependent priority queues (EDCA access categories for ITS-G5), so safety-critical messages (e.g. DENMs) can preempt background traffic. See the Access Layer page for EDCA details.

Basic Transport Protocol (BTP) The Basic Transport Protocol (BTP) sits directly above GeoNetworking (EN 302 636-5-1 / TS 103 836-5-1). Its sole job is port-based multiplexing and demultiplexing of facility-layer messages — analogous to UDP in the IP world, but even simpler: no checksum, no flow control, no connection state. The entire BTP header is exactly 4 bytes . 4 bytes BTP header size smallest transport header in any major stack 16-bit Port numbers well-known ports defined in ETSI TS 103 248 2 types BTP-A and BTP-B interactive vs non-interactive BTP-A vs BTP-B BTP-A (4 B) Destination port 16 bit Source port 16 bit BTP-A header (4 bytes): destination port + source port BTP-B (4 B) Destination port 16 bit Destination port info 16 bit BTP-B header (4 bytes): destination port + destination port info Property BTP-A (interactive) BTP-B (non-interactive) NH encoding in Common Header 1 2 Header bytes 4: Destination port (16b) + Source port (16b) 4: Destination port (16b) + Destination port info (16b) Source port Present — the port a reply should be directed to Absent Destination port info Absent Present — additional qualifier for well-known ports (per TS 103 248) Use case Request-response exchanges, session-based facilities Broadcast / anycast: CAM, DENM, CPM, VAM — one-way dissemination BTP header types (EN 302 636-5-1, clause 7) ● Which type does CAM use? CAM (and most other periodic safety messages) use BTP-B . There is no need for a source port because CAMs are not replied-to; the GeoNetworking source position vector already identifies the sender. BTP-A is reserved for protocol exchanges that genuinely require a reply endpoint. Well-known BTP port assignments Port assignments are standardised in ETSI TS 103 248 BTP Port Numbers . A subset of the most commonly deployed ports: Port Message / Service Standard 2001 CAM — Cooperative Awareness Message EN 302 637-2 / TS 103 900 2002 DENM — Decentralised Environmental Notification Message EN 302 637-3 / TS 103 831 2003 MAPEM — MAP Extended Message TS 103 301 2004 SPATEM — Signal Phase and Timing Extended Message TS 103 301 2005 SAEM — Service Announcement Extended Message TS 102 890-1 2006 IVIM — Infrastructure to Vehicle Information Message TS 103 301 2009 RTCMEM — RTCM Extended Message (GNSS corrections) TS 103 301 2010 CPM — Collective Perception Message TS 103 324 2018 VAM — Vulnerable Road User Awareness Message TS 103 300-3 2030 SREM — Signal Request Extended Message TS 103 301 2031 SSEM — Signal Request Status Extended Message TS 103 301 2045 MCM — Manoeuvre Coordination Message TS 103 461 BTP well-known port assignments (ETSI TS 103 248) How BTP works end-to-end 1 Facility layer requests transmission : e.g. the CAM service calls BTP-Data.request with BTP type=BTP-B, Destination port=2001, GN transport type=SHB, Traffic class=0 (highest priority). 2 BTP adds its 4-byte header : Destination port (2001) + Destination port info (0 for CAM). The combined BTP-PDU is passed to GeoNetworking via the GN-SAP using GN-Data.request. 3 GeoNetworking encapsulates : adds Basic Header (LT, RHL), Common Header (NH=2 for BTP-B, HT=5/HST=0 for SHB, TC), and SHB Extended Header (Source LPV). Sets MAC destination address to broadcast. 4 Access layer transmits : ITS-G5 frame (Ethertype 0x8947 identifies GeoNetworking) carries the complete stack over the 5.9 GHz channel. 5 Receiver demultiplexes : GeoNetworking strips its headers, passes the BTP-PDU upward via GN-Data.indication. BTP reads Destination port=2001 and delivers the payload to the CAM service.

IPv6 over GeoNetworking (GN6ASL) EN 302 636-6-1 specifies the GeoNetworking to IPv6 Adaptation Sub-Layer (GN6ASL) . It allows standard IPv6 stacks — without any modification — to send and receive packets over the GeoNetworking network. From the IPv6 perspective, all ITS stations appear to be attached to the same virtual Ethernet link. GN6ASL is signalled in the Common Header NH field as value 3 (IPv6) . It presents virtual network interfaces of Ethernet V2.0/IEEE 802.3 type to IPv6, with the 48-bit MAC address derived from the MID field of the local GN_ADDR. Virtual link types Geographical Virtual Link (GVL) A link-local multicast-capable virtual link with geographically scoped boundaries tied to a GBC/GAC area. Supports IPv6 Neighbour Discovery (ND) and SLAAC. Two sub-types: Static GVL (area set by RSU management or derived from a received Router Advertisement) and Dynamic GVL (area assigned per-packet via the experimental EGN6_SAP). Topological Virtual Link (TVL) A link-local multicast-capable virtual link with topologically scoped boundaries (based on TSB). Does not guarantee symmetric reachability; IPv6 ND is disabled on TVLs. One TVL exists per GeoNetworking interface. Key capabilities enabled by GN6ASL: IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (SLAAC, RFC 4862) over Static GVLs IPv6 Neighbour Discovery over SGVLs (Router Advertisement / Solicitation / Neighbour Solicitation) Sub-IP multi-hop delivery of IPv6 packets (GeoNetworking forwards the packet; IPv6 Hop Limit is not decremented at each GeoNetworking hop) IPv6 multicast via GeoBroadcast (geocasting of IPv6 multicast traffic) Network Mobility Basic Support (NEMO BS, RFC 3963) for in-vehicle mobile routers The MTU available to IPv6 (MTU_GN6) equals the access layer MTU (MTU_AL) minus the size of the largest GeoNetworking header (GEO_MAX), expressed as: MTU_GN6 = min(MTU_VI, MTU_AL - GEO_MAX) . For ITS-G5 with its 1 500-byte Ethernet frame this typically gives IPv6 payloads of around 1 300–1 400 bytes. ● GN6ASL vs BTP BTP and GN6ASL are alternatives at the same layer position, both directly above GeoNetworking. BTP is used by native ITS facility messages (CAM, DENM, …). GN6ASL is used when an ITS station needs to carry conventional Internet traffic (TCP/UDP/HTTPS) over the vehicular network. Both coexist peacefully — a vehicle can exchange CAMs over BTP while downloading a firmware update over IPv6/GN6ASL.

Beaconing The BEACON packet (HT=1, SHB delivery) is a housekeeping mechanism: it carries no payload but lets a GeoAdhoc router announce its presence and broadcast its Long Position Vector to neighbours. This keeps the LocT current even when the station is not sending any data packets. Key properties: Transmitted as SHB — exactly one wireless transmission, no forwarding. Interval governed by itsGnBeaconServiceRetransmitTimer. When a station is actively sending CAMs or other messages that already embed a Source LPV, those packets effectively serve as implicit beacons, and the explicit BEACON rate may be reduced or suppressed to avoid redundant channel load. DCC may further back off the beacon rate under high channel load conditions. ● CAMs as implicit beacons In practice, vehicles send CAMs at 1–10 Hz. Each CAM's SHB Extended Header carries a full Long Position Vector, so active vehicles rarely need explicit BEACON packets. The explicit BEACON is mainly useful for stationary RSUs or vehicles that happen to have no application traffic at the moment.

Media-independent vs media-dependent split The GeoNetworking specification is deliberately divided into two parts to allow the core protocol to work over multiple radio access technologies: Media-Independent (EN 302 636-4-1 / TS 103 836-4-1) Defines all packet formats (Basic Header, Common Header, Extended Headers), forwarding algorithms (greedy, CBF, area CBF, advanced), data structures (LocT, LS buffer, forwarding buffer, CBF buffer), address format, security integration (TS 103 097 hooks), duplicate packet detection, and the complete protocol state machine. This part is access-technology agnostic. Media-Dependent (e.g. EN 302 636-4-2 for ITS-G5) Specifies how GeoNetworking Traffic Classes map to the access-layer priority queues (EDCA), encapsulation in 802.11p frames using Ethertype 0x8947, power and rate settings, and technology-specific forwarding heuristics. A separate media-dependent part exists for LTE-V2X (ETSI TS 103 613). This split means the same forwarding algorithm and packet format works equally on ITS-G5 and on C-V2X sidelink, with only the encapsulation layer differing. Hybrid vehicles supporting both radios can use a single GeoNetworking address and forward packets over the best available interface.

Release 1 vs Release 2 (TS 103 836 series) The TS 103 836 series (Release 2) supersedes and extends the EN 302 636 Release 1 family. Release 2 was developed to align with the EU Delegated Regulation on C-ITS, support newer message types (CPM, VAM, MCM), and incorporate technical corrections accumulated over years of conformance testing. Aspect Release 1 (EN 302 636 series) Release 2 (TS 103 836 series) Document type European Standard (EN) Technical Specification (TS), to become EN in due course GeoNetworking core EN 302 636-4-1 V1.4.1 (2020) TS 103 836-4-1 V2.2.1 (2026) BTP EN 302 636-5-1 V2.2.1 (2019) TS 103 836-5-1 V2.1.1 (2024) Packet format Baseline — defines the bit-level format Identical on the wire — backward compatible with R1 Port numbers reference ETSI TS 103 248 (Release 1) ETSI TS 103 248 Release 2 (updated port list) New capabilities GUC, GBC, GAC, SHB, TSB, beaconing, LS Refined protocol constants; expanded ITS-AID/SSP profiles; aligned with newer security standards (TS 103 097 v2) Key differences between GeoNetworking Release 1 and Release 2 ● Backward compatibility Release 2 GeoNetworking packets are bit-for-bit identical in format to Release 1 packets. A Release 1 vehicle and a Release 2 vehicle interoperate seamlessly at the GeoNetworking/BTP layer. The Release distinction matters primarily for the facility-layer message profiles and security profiles that travel inside the payload, not for the network layer itself.

FACILITIES LAYER Facilities Layer: Messages, Data & Services The facilities layer is the intelligence of the ITS station. Sitting between the networking stack and applications, it creates and processes all C-ITS messages, maintains a shared dictionary of common data types, runs a local sensor-fused map of the surroundings, and manages the station's position and time reference. Every message — from CAM to DENM to CPM — originates and terminates here. ETSI TS 102 894-1 V2.0.0 ETSI TS 102 894-2 V2.4.1 ETSI EN 302 895 V1.1.1 ETSI EN 302 890-2 V2.1.1 ETSI EN 302 890-1 V1.1.1 Role in the ITS-S Architecture An ITS Station (ITS-S) is structured according to the reference architecture defined in ETSI EN 302 665 ITS Communications Architecture . It has four horizontal layers — access, networking & transport, facilities, and applications — plus two vertical cross-layers (management and security). The facilities layer occupies the critical middle tier: Security Applications CA, DEN, CP, VRU, Platooning, GLOSA … Facilities Layer Message services · CDD · LDM · PoTi · SA Networking & Transport GeoNetworking · BTP · IPv6 Access Layer ITS-G5 · C-V2X · LTE-V · DSRC Management The facilities layer is responsible for: Encoding and decoding all ITS message PDUs (Protocol Data Units) using ASN.1 / UPER. Providing the Common Data Dictionary (CDD) — a shared library of data types reused by every message. Operating the Local Dynamic Map (LDM) — a timestamped, geo-referenced database of nearby objects and events. Delivering authoritative position and time information to all other layers through the PoTi entity. Running service management facilities such as the Services Announcement (SA) service. ● Why a separate facilities layer? Without the facilities layer, every application would have to implement its own message codec, its own position engine, and its own neighbour database. The facilities layer centralises these costly functions once per ITS-S and exposes them to any number of concurrent applications through well-defined service access points (FA-SAP, NF-SAP, MF-SAP, SF-SAP). The structure is governed at a high level by ETSI TS 102 894-1 Facility Layer Structure R2 , which defines the Release 2 functional architecture. Release 2 (version 2.Y.Z) specifications are self-consistent and backward compatible with Release 1 at the PDU level — a Release 1 receiver can decode a Release 2 message, provided no breaking extension markers were added. Common Data Dictionary (CDD) ETSI TS 102 894-2 CDD Release 2 defines the ITS Common Data Dictionary — a repository of Data Elements (DEs) and Data Frames (DFs) that any ITS message can import instead of defining its own types. The CDD removes the need for every standard to invent its own representation of "position" or "speed", ensures semantic interoperability, and simplifies conformance testing. ● Data Elements vs Data Frames A Data Element (DE) is a primitive, atomic value — an integer, enumeration or bit string with a precise unit and range. A Data Frame (DF) is a structured composite of DEs and/or other DFs, analogous to a struct in C. The CDD defines both. CDD Structure The entire CDD is encoded as a single ASN.1 module named ETSI-ITS-CDD , identified by the Object Identifier: {itu-t (0) identified-organization (4) etsi (0) itsDomain (5) wg1 (1) 102894 cdd (2) major-version-4 (4) minor-version-3 (3)} The module uses ASN.1 with UPER (Unaligned Packed Encoding Rules) for compact over-the-air transmission. Each DE or DF carries an in-module semantic comment following the Javadoc-style template: @brief , @param / @field , @unit , @category , and @revision . DE/DF Categories Every CDD data object belongs to at least one of the following categories, which help implementers locate relevant types: Basic Information Elementary values — protocol version, message ID, station ID, timestamps. Vehicle Information Types specific to road and rail vehicles — vehicle dimensions, vehicle role, light status. GeoReference Information Geographic descriptions — reference position, altitude, relevance area shapes. Kinematic Information Motion state — speed, heading, curvature, acceleration, yaw rate, path history. Traffic & Road Topology Road events, cause codes, traffic participant types, intersection topology. Sensing & VRU Information Sensor data, detected objects, cluster information, Vulnerable Road User profiles. CDD Versioning The CDD has evolved through four Release 2 versions. The major-version arc in the OID is incremented only when backward compatibility of encoded PDUs is broken (e.g. a type is renamed or fields are reordered). Adding a new DE/DF, or adding a field at the end of an extensible SEQUENCE, increments only the minor-version and does not break existing decoders. Current version is V2.4.1 (2025-11) . Local Dynamic Map (LDM) ETSI EN 302 895 Local Dynamic Map defines the LDM — a conceptual, timestamped, geo-referenced data store residing within an ITS-S that aggregates information from all sources (received messages, on-board sensors, applications) and serves it to authorised consumers on demand or by subscription. The LDM does not modify provider data. It is not a communication protocol — it is a well-defined internal service accessed via four interfaces. Conceptual Layers Conceptually the data held in the LDM can be organised into four layers of increasing dynamicity: 4 Dynamic Events Received DENMs, hazard alerts, road-work zones — transient events with explicit time validity periods. Provided by the DEN basic service. 3 Mobile Objects Nearby vehicles, VRUs, RSUs — data from received CAMs, VAMs, CPMs. Expires quickly (order of seconds) if not refreshed. 2 Transient Data Traffic signals (SPATEM/MAPEM), intersection maps, road-side information — semi-static but updated periodically by infrastructure. 1 Static Map Data Road network geometry, lane topology, speed limits, static POIs — long-lived background map layer used for context. LDM conceptual data layers — from static map to dynamic events LDM Functional Architecture EN 302 895 defines two internal components and four external interfaces: FN.LDM.1 — LDM Service Handles registration/deregistration of Data Providers and Data Consumers, processes query and publish/subscribe requests, and enforces access authorisation. FN.LDM.2 — LDM Maintenance Stores LDM Data Objects, applies time-validity and geo-validity rules (LDM Area of Maintenance), and performs garbage collection of expired objects. C-ITS Message Taxonomy Every message produced at the facilities layer shares the same top-level structure: an ItsPduHeader (from the CDD) followed by a message-specific body. The messageId field of the header identifies the message type. The table below catalogues the principal message types in Release 1 and Release 2. CAM DENM Decentralised Environmental Notification Message ETSI TS 103 831 (R2) Event-driven alert — accident, roadworks, hazard. Geographically targeted, time-limited. DENM CPM Collective Perception Message ETSI TS 103 324 Sensor-detected object sharing — lets vehicles act as distributed sensors for each other. CPM VAM VRU Awareness Message ETSI TS 103 300-3 (R2) Presence and kinematics of Vulnerable Road Users (pedestrians, cyclists, personal mobility). Infrastructure SREM Signal Request Extended Message ETSI TS 103 301 (R2) Vehicle requests priority or pre-emption at a signalised intersection.
