sectionTitle: C-Roads Roadmap: From Day-1 to Automated Driving
text: C-Roads Roadmap: From Day-1 to Automated Driving The C-Roads Roadmap (v1.0, April 2024) is not a projection of future specifications — it describes use cases that have already been implemented and tested, giving OEMs and infrastructure managers a view of what is "ready to market" and what is coming next. All published C-Roads use cases have been validated in real-world pilot deployments before publication. ✅ Now operational Road Works Warning (all variants), Hazardous Location Notifications (14 use cases), In-Vehicle Signage (5 use cases), Signalized Intersection services (GLOSA, SPTI, TLP, ISVW, EVP), Probe Vehicle Data. These are in regular operational use across multiple member states. 🚗 ADAS integration The same Day-1 services feed Advanced Driver Assistance Systems. Digitalisation of (1) hazard warnings, (2) regulatory traffic signs including VMS, and (3) traffic signals makes these available as structured inputs to ADAS and L2+ automation functions — not just for driver information. 🤖 Automated driving (Day-2) Complex roadworks zone topology (detailed work zone layout for automated vehicles), Automated Vehicle Guidance (AVG), Collective Perception Message (CPM) integration, and Topology Information (TI) are in pre-deployment evaluation. These require higher-precision IVIM content and/or CPM from infrastructure. The roadmap emphasises deployment synergies : a city that installs RSUs at intersections for public transport priority has already deployed the physical and logical infrastructure to support emergency vehicle priority, GLOSA for private vehicles, and VRU warnings — each additional service requires only software configuration, not new hardware. This layered approach lowers the marginal cost of adding use cases once the first deployment is in place. Trust between infrastructure and vehicles is managed via the C-ITS Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) . The ECTL (European Certificate Trust List) is the root of cross-border trust: an RSU's pseudonym certificate, issued by an Authorisation Authority (AA) enrolled in the ECTL, is trusted by any vehicle whose OBU root certificate is also in the ECTL. Austria's 2024 ECTL L1 achievement — covering all RSUs and trailers — is the first major member state to reach this operational milestone.

sectionTitle: Relationships: ETSI, CAR 2 CAR, and EU Policy
text: Relationships: ETSI, CAR 2 CAR, and EU Policy C-Roads does not operate in isolation. It sits at the intersection of standards bodies, industry consortia, and EU regulatory frameworks: ETSI (profiling relationship) C-Roads profiles ETSI EN 302 637-2 (CAM), EN 302 637-3 (DENM), TS 103 301 (infrastructure facilities), TS 103 097 (security), and the ITS Data Dictionary (TS 102 894-2). Every C-Roads data element is defined in the ETSI standards; C-Roads restricts or selects values. When ETSI updates a standard, C-Roads aligns its profile in the next release. CAR 2 CAR Communication Consortium (C2C-CC) The vehicle-side counterpart. C2C-CC produces the Basic System Profile (BSP) and vehicle OBU specifications. C-Roads and C2C-CC coordinate closely: the C-Roads Message Profiles document was explicitly "aligned with BSP 1.4" in Release 1.6. This alignment ensures that RSU-broadcast messages conform to what OEM vehicles expect, and vice versa. EU Commission / EU Policy The EU C-ITS Platform (Phase I and II) defined the initial Day-1 service list and the European Certificate Policy (CP) and Security Policy (SP). C-Roads operationalises these: it deploys the Day-1 services the Commission identified and implements the EU CP in its PKI architecture. The ITS Delegated Regulation (which stalled in 2019 before finally progressing) created uncertainty for deployments; C-Roads provided continuity during that period. ISO (data standards) IVI messages use CEN ISO/TS 19321 data elements (IVIM message content) and ISO 14823 pictogram codes for sign types (e.g. code 557 = Maximum speed limit). The AMQP publisherId registration uses EN ISO 14816. C-Roads profiles reference these ISO standards where the ETSI message content itself draws on ISO. Vehicle Industry CAR 2 CAR Communication Consortium The CAR 2 CAR Communication Consortium (C2C-CC) is the vehicle-industry side of European C-ITS — a non-commercial association of vehicle manufacturers, Tier-1 suppliers, and research organisations that defines exactly what a car, truck, motorcycle or e-bike must do to participate in Europe's cooperative road-safety system. Its master specification, the Basic System Profile (BSP), pins down every interoperability requirement from antenna power to authorization-ticket rotation, so vehicles from competing brands communicate seamlessly the moment they leave the factory. C2CCC RS 2035 C2CCC RS 2036 C2CCC RS 2037 C2CCC TR 2000 C2CCC WP 2072 What is the C2C-CC? Founded in 2002 by vehicle manufacturers who believed cooperative road traffic could save lives, the CAR 2 CAR Communication Consortium (C2C-CC) is today the authoritative voice of the automotive industry in European Cooperative Intelligent Transport Systems (C-ITS). Its members include worldwide major vehicle manufacturers (OEMs), equipment suppliers, and research organisations. The consortium's primary objective is to ensure interoperability in C-ITS between different vehicle manufacturers and with road infrastructure — an engineering challenge that means every car, truck, bus, motorcycle, e-bike, and even agricultural machine carrying a C-ITS station must transmit and receive in a mutually intelligible way regardless of make, model, or country of sale. C2C-CC members focus on wireless Vehicle-to-Vehicle (V2V) communication based on the Direct Communication paradigm (no cloud intermediate required), with Vehicle-to-Infrastructure (V2I) as an equally important companion. ● Core mandate C2C-CC specifies the vehicle side of European C-ITS. Its counterpart for the road side is the C-Roads platform . Together they form the two pillars of European interoperability: OEM-specified vehicle stations meeting infrastructure-specified roadside stations. 2002 Founded by European vehicle OEMs ITS-G5 Primary radio technology 5 855–5 925 MHz band 500 000+ C-ITS-equipped vehicles commercially deployed by 2022 Relationships: ETSI, C-Roads and EU Policy C2C-CC does not write standards in isolation — it feeds into and draws from a wider ecosystem: ETSI TC ITS The European Telecommunications Standards Institute's ITS technical committee produces the normative standards (EN 302 xxx, TS 103 xxx) that C2C-CC profiles and mandates. C2C-CC members contribute heavily to ETSI work items, ensuring that ETSI standards reflect what automotive OEMs actually need to build deployable products. C-Roads platform C-Roads is the road-operator equivalent — national transport ministries and road authorities specifying what a roadside C-ITS station (RSU) must do. C2C-CC and C-Roads work under a signed Memorandum of Understanding to harmonise their specifications so that vehicle CAMs and DENMs generated by the BSP profile are correctly understood by roadside stations, and vice versa. EU policy The EU ITS Directive (2010/40/EC and amendments), the Amsterdam Declaration on cooperative and automated driving, and the European Commission's C-ITS strategy all lean on C2C-CC and C-Roads work as the technical foundation. The C2C-CC BSP was referenced in draft EU delegated acts on C-ITS deployment. EuroNCAP The independent vehicle safety assessment body has already recognised the C-ITS Day-1 local hazard warning application in its safety ratings and included C-ITS in its long-term 2025 and 2027 roadmaps — creating a market pull for BSP-compliant vehicles. The Basic System Profile (BSP) The BSP is C2C-CC's master specification — a release bundle of interconnected documents that together define the minimum interoperable vehicle C-ITS system. The BSP does three things: it names the ETSI (and other) standards that apply; it profiles those standards (selecting specific options, forbidding others); and it adds concrete implementation requirements where the standards leave room for variation. The BSP is structured as a three-layer requirement hierarchy mirroring the abstraction levels from goals down to testable behaviour: 1 Objectives (RS 2035) — abstract, non-testable goals such as "improve road safety towards Vision Zero" or "protect privacy under GDPR". Each objective is further detailed by one or more features or feature requests. 2 Features (RS 2036) — desired abilities of the vehicle C-ITS station. For example, "provide services for communicating with other C-ITS stations using the vehicular ad-hoc RLAN in 5 855–5 925 MHz" or "implement backward-compatible facility-layer services and messages". A feature is assumed tested when all its detailing requirements are tested. 3 Vehicle C-ITS Station Profile (RS 2037) — the lowest level: concrete, testable requirements with numeric parameters. This is where interoperability actually lives — RF power, GeoNetworking field values, CAM generation rates, ECDSA key sizes, authorization-ticket rotation distances, clock tolerances. ● Backward compatibility is a first-class requirement RS_OBJ_00440 mandates that every Release 2 vehicle C-ITS station is backward compatible with Release 1 stations and C-Roads Release 2.x.y — a newer vehicle must provide at least the same service level as an older one in an older environment, and older vehicles must retain full functionality in a newer-release environment. RS 2035 — Objectives Sets the abstract "why": Vision Zero, ad-hoc low-latency local comms, GDPR privacy, misbehaviour detection, functional safety, EU-wide trusted network. Objectives detail the full vehicle type scope: cars, trucks, buses, PTWs, e-bikes, cycles, agricultural machines, rail vehicles. RS 2036 — Features Specifies the "what": multi-channel radio access, DCC congestion avoidance, CEN-DSRC interference mitigation, CAM/DENM facility services, CPM perception sharing, GNSS + confidence information, certificate-based authentication, AT pseudonym rotation, misbehaviour reporting, ASIL safety containers. RS 2037 — Profile Defines the "how" with numeric requirements: G5-SCH0 at 5 900 MHz (6 Mbit/s default), CAM on Single Hop Broadcast, DENM on GeoBroadcast, GN address anonymous mode, ECDSA P-256 signatures, AT rotation every 800–1 500 m then 10–20 km then 25–35 km intervals, clock valid within 20 ms of C-ITS time (TAI since 2004-01-01), RF power 17–33 dBm e.i.r.p. Provide the formal security assurance framework on top of ETSI PKI requirements. Day-1 Safety Use Cases The C2C-CC roadmap organises deployment in phases named Day 1, Day 2, and Day 3+. Day 1 — the current live phase — is called Awareness Driving : vehicles transmit their own status and event-triggered hazard warnings to increase the spatial and temporal awareness horizon for drivers and vehicle systems. All Day-1 vehicle-originated use cases rely on two ETSI facility-layer services: Cooperative Awareness Service (CA) — generates CAMs at 1–10 Hz adaptively based on vehicle dynamics and channel load; Single Hop Broadcast (SHB). Decentralised Environmental Notification Service (DEN) — generates DENMs on event detection; GeoBroadcast (GBC), multi-hop over the relevance area, repeated as long as the event is valid. Use Case Triggering Document Message(s) Notes Stationary Vehicle Warning RS 2006 (tcStVe) DENM Broken-down vehicle, accident stopped; speed ≤ 0.08 m/s for cars, ≤ 1.4 m/s for PTW Slow Vehicle / Traffic-Jam Warning RS 2007 (tcTrJa) DENM Tail-of-queue approaching warning; relative speed delta detection Adverse Weather Conditions RS 2002 (tcAdWe) DENM Icy road, low visibility, reduced friction detected by ESC / rain sensor Dangerous Situation (Emergency Brake) RS 2003 (tcDaSi) DENM Emergency brake (eCall trigger), pre-crash imminent collision alert Special / Emergency Vehicle Warning RS 2005 (tcSpVe) DENM Blue-light vehicles, roadworks vehicles, road-operator trailers Wrong-way Driver (Ghost Driver) RS 2322 (tcWWD) DENM Counter-flow driving on motorway detected by heading vs lane map Unresponsive Driver RS 2321 (tcURD) DENM Vehicle driving erratically; triggers eCall assistance chain Motorcycle Approaching Information (MAI) CAM profile (PTW) CAM Day-1 PTW presence beaconing using existing CAM format Exchange of In-Road Characters (IRC) RS 2004 (tcIRC) DENM Road surface condition sharing (wetness, ice, debris) In-Vehicle Signage / GLOSA (received) C-Roads SPATEM/MAPEM SPATEM, MAPEM, IVIM Infrastructure → vehicle; vehicle BSP profiles the receive side Day-1 C-ITS safety and efficiency use cases as defined by C2C-CC BSP triggering-condition documents ● Use-case triggering is transmitter-side; applications are receiver-side The BSP and triggering-condition documents define exactly how a vehicle detects and announces an event — which CAN signals to monitor, which thresholds to apply, how to fill DENM fields. What the receiving vehicle does with that information (warn the driver, apply autonomous braking, update a map) is intentionally left to the OEM to allow competitive differentiation while maintaining liability clarity.

Key Technical Parameters (RS 2037 Profile) The Vehicle C-ITS Station Profile (RS 2037) contains a normative parameter table (Table 3 in the document) that fixes concrete numeric values for the entire protocol stack. Key parameters: Parameter Value Unit Meaning G5-SCH0 (primary channel) 5 900 MHz, ch. 180 MHz Default service channel for CAMs and priority C-ITS services pAlDataRateSch0 6 Mbit/s Default data rate on SCH0; range 3–27 Mbit/s RF output power target 23 (range 17–33) dBm e.i.r.p. Nominal transmit power; max 33 dBm with ≥30 dB TPC range pPotiMaxTimeDiff 20 ms Max offset between station clock and C-ITS TAI time pPotiUpdateRate 10 Hz GNSS position-and-time update rate pCamGenNumber 3 msgs CAMs that may be generated without time-interval restrictions pCamPathMaxLength / MinLength 500 / 200 m Bounds on CAM path history length pDenmTraceMaxLength / MinLength 1 000 / 600 m Bounds on DENM trace path length pDenmTraceMaxPoints 40 points Max trace points in DENMs pGnMaxAreaSize 80 km² Maximum GeoNetworking GeoBroadcast area size pSecMaxAcceptDistance 10 km Max sender–receiver distance for message acceptance (6 hops × 1 km) pSecCamPastToleranceTime 2 s Max age of CAM timestamp accepted at receiver pSecMessagePastToleranceTime 10 min Max age of non-CAM message timestamp accepted pSecMaxPreloadTime 3 months Max AT preload time (2 weeks for aftermarket supervised OBUs) AT rotation #1 (after ignition on) 800–1 500 m First pseudonym change; random in range AT rotation #2 10 000–20 000 m Second rotation interval AT rotation #3+ (steady state) 25 000–35 000 m Subsequent steady-state pseudonym rotation interval Min. AT pool for signing 56 ATs Must hold ≥56 valid ATs + private keys before signing any message pSecChangeBlockingMaxTime 5 min Max time an application can delay AT rotation while vehicle moves GN address mode ANONYMOUS (2) — GN source address configured anonymously for privacy (pGnAddrConfMode) pGnEtherType 0x8947 — EtherType for GeoNetworking frames pBtpCamPort 2 001 — Well-known BTP destination port for CAM pBtpDenmPort 2 002 — Well-known BTP destination port for DENM Selected normative parameters from C2C-CC RS 2037 BSP Release 2.0.2 ● Authorization ticket rotation and privacy The AT rotation protocol is specifically engineered to prevent vehicle tracking. A new random Authorization Ticket (AT pseudonym certificate) is selected from a pool of at least 56 at every ignition restart (after at least 10 min off), then again after 800–1 500 m, then at 10–20 km, and thereafter every 25–35 km of travel. At each rotation, the GN source address, DENM trace storage, CAM path history, and all transmitted identifiers are simultaneously replaced to defeat correlation attacks. See Security for the full CCMS architecture.

sectionTitle: C2C-CC Deployment Roadmap: Day 1 to Day 3+
text: C2C-CC Deployment Roadmap: Day 1 to Day 3+ The C2C-CC organises the evolution of C-ITS into successive deployment phases. Each phase inherits all capabilities of the previous phase in a backward-compatible manner — newer vehicles continue to transmit information needed by older vehicles. New services and supporting functionalities are layered on top, not replacing them. 👁️ Day 1 — Awareness Driving Now live. Vehicles share their own dynamics (CAM at 1–10 Hz) and hazard alerts (DENM). Infrastructure supplies SPATEM/MAPEM and IVIM. Applications warn drivers of hazards beyond line of sight. First deployed: VW Golf 8 in 2019; 500 000+ vehicles and 20 000 km of roads equipped by 2022. Services: CA (CAM), DEN (DENM), TLM, RLT, IVI 📡 Day 2 — Sensing Driving Standards in progress. Vehicles with environment sensors (radar, lidar, camera) share detected objects via CPM and VRU alerts via VAM . Enables awareness of non-equipped road users (pedestrians, cyclists) around corners. Semi-automated reactions (cooperative emergency braking, C-ACC) become possible. Requires CPM object quality metrics, functional-safety ASIL containers, and misbehaviour detection. New services: CP (CPM), VRU Awareness (VAM) 🤖 Day 3+ — Cooperative Driving R&D phase. SAE Level 3–4 automated vehicles share trajectories and coordinate manoeuvres (cooperative lane change, merging, advanced C-ACC). Infrastructure may provide trajectory suggestions, gap advisories, minimum-risk-manoeuvre notifications, and valet-parking guidance. VRUs become active V2X participants. MCM / Manoeuvre Coordination is a key enabler. New services: MCM, IMZM, advanced SPATEM ● The ISAD framework for infrastructure readiness The roadmap uses the Infrastructure Support Levels for Automated Driving (ISAD) to classify road infrastructure capability at each phase. ISAD Level C (static and dynamic road info for human drivers) maps to Day 1; higher ISAD levels providing perception data and trajectory guidance map to Day 2 and Day 3+ respectively.

sectionTitle: Protection Profiles: Common Criteria Security Evaluation
text: Protection Profiles: Common Criteria Security Evaluation Beyond operational requirements, C2C-CC publishes two Common Criteria (CC) Protection Profiles that define the security assurance requirements for the hardware and software components of a vehicle C-ITS station. These allow OEMs and suppliers to obtain independent third-party security evaluations against a standardised target. 🔐 PP 2056 — V2X Hardware Security Module (HSM) The Protection Profile for the V2X HSM defines security functional requirements and assurance level for the dedicated cryptographic hardware that stores private keys, generates ECDSA signatures, and manages the AT pool inside a vehicle C-ITS station. The HSM must resist physical tampering and logical attacks, ensuring that private keys cannot be extracted even if the surrounding vehicle ECU is compromised. CC evaluation against this PP provides the hardware-level trust anchor for the entire C-ITS PKI chain. 🛡️ PP 2302 — Vehicle C-ITS Station (VCS) The Protection Profile for the complete Vehicle C-ITS Station defines security targets for the full station software and hardware combination — encompassing message signing/verification, AT lifecycle management, privacy protection through pseudonym rotation, misbehaviour detection interfaces, and the secure channel between the C-ITS station and the in-vehicle network. CC evaluation against VCS PP provides assurance that the deployed station correctly implements the C2C-CC security requirements from RS 2037. ● Relationship to ETSI security standards The Protection Profiles complement rather than replace the ETSI security standards. RS 2037 requires compliance with the European C-ITS Certificate Policy, the C-ITS Security Policy, and ETSI TS 103 097 ITS security header and certificate formats , TS 102 940 ITS security architecture and management , and TS 102 941 Trust and privacy management . The C2C-CC PPs add Common Criteria methodology and an independent evaluator into the trust chain. See Security for the full CCMS picture.

Europe's Path to CCAM C2C-CC's 2022 position paper C-ITS: Europe's Path to Connected, Cooperative & Automated Mobility articulates the industry's long-term vision and policy asks. Key themes: C-ITS as public infrastructure C2C-CC argues that C-ITS creates a public communications infrastructure analogous to the road network itself, on which future automation depends. It is specified by those who operate it — automotive manufacturers and road operators — is based on open accessible standards, and is designed to keep licence costs at minimum. Interoperability and backward compatibility as non-negotiables The LEGO-brick metaphor: C-ITS transmitters "click" only if they follow the same specification. Backward compatibility means a plug made in 1990 works with sockets from 1965 and 2022 alike — vehicles sold today must still benefit from C-ITS infrastructure built decades from now, and vice versa. ITS-G5 delivers Day-1 now The position paper states that ITS-G5 fully delivers Day-1 use cases. Industry welcomes evolution of the physical layer (IEEE 802.11bd, potential cellular complementary technology) but insists that service continuity and backward compatibility must be preserved across any technology transition. EuroNCAP recognition as market driver EuroNCAP's recognition of "local hazard warning" (a Day-1 ITS-G5 application) in its safety ratings creates a concrete commercial incentive for OEMs to equip vehicles with BSP-compliant C-ITS stations. EuroNCAP's 2025 and 2027 roadmaps both include C-ITS commitments. Cooperative sensing bridges the automation gap Day-2 Collective Perception (CPM) allows a vehicle's sensors to become a shared resource for the network. An automated vehicle that "sees" a pedestrian hidden around a corner can share that perception with approaching vehicles — bridging the line-of-sight limitation that prevents purely on-board sensors from enabling higher automation levels safely. Policy asks C2C-CC calls on EU regulators to protect 5.9 GHz spectrum, maintain backward-compatibility requirements in the ITS Directive, support the European C-ITS security framework (CCMS / CPOC), and engage OEMs and road operators in the governance of the C-ITS ecosystem. See the EU Policy page for details.

Vehicle Type Coverage: Release 2 Expansion C2C-CC Release 2 significantly expands the vehicle scope beyond the car-centric Release 1. The definition of "vehicle C-ITS station" in RS_OBJ_00149 now explicitly covers: Cars & light commercials UNECE categories M1, N1 (passenger cars and vans). The original focus of Release 1; most BSP requirements are written for the car case with explicit profile tags. Trucks & heavy commercials UNECE categories N2 and N3. Platooning and freight use cases; specific CAM profiling for trailer length (VehicleLengthConfidenceIndication = trailerPresentWithKnownLength). Buses UNECE categories M2 and M3; priority-vehicle and public-transport use cases. Powered Two-Wheelers (PTW) EU Regulation [EU R168] categories L1e-B and L3e. Significant new profiling in R2.0.2: separate stationary-speed threshold ( <= 1.4 m/s vs <= 0.08 m/s for cars), PTW-specific heading latch thresholds, no stored heading at start-up, distinct regular-driving-dynamics bounds (lateral acceleration < 1.9 m/s², longitudinal deceleration > -2.4 m/s²). E-bikes & Cycles EPACs ( ≤ 25 km/h EU), S-EPACs ( ≤ 45 km/h), throttle-assist bikes. Cycles get a dedicated "cycle in use" state machine: detection duration 2 s, timeout 300 s, to prevent CAM transmission when the cycle is transported in a car or on a train. Agricultural & rail UNECE category T agricultural machines; rail vehicles (trams and urban rail as studied in TR 2053). Trailers and drones are listed as "to be decided". Indicates the ambition to cover all moving road and track users over successive releases. ● Partial implementation is explicitly allowed A vehicle C-ITS station from any category is not required to implement every feature. However, if a feature or requirement is implemented, it must be fully compliant with the C2C-CC specification — partial compliance of a mandatory requirement is not permitted.

EU REGULATORY FRAMEWORK EU Policy & Regulation for C-ITS European C-ITS deployment is shaped by a layered policy framework stretching from a 2010 framework directive through stakeholder expert groups, a 2016 deployment strategy, and a proposed 2019 delegated regulation that was rejected by the Council — leaving harmonised deployment in the hands of the C-Roads platform rather than binding EU law. ITS Directive 2010/40/EU COM(2016) 766 C(2019) 1789 draft The Core Policy Tension ● No binding C-ITS delegated act exists Despite years of preparation, the 2019 draft Delegated Regulation C(2019) 1789 was rejected by the Council of the EU. The principal dispute was technology neutrality: the draft mandated ITS-G5 (ETSI 802.11p-based) as the short-range baseline, which Member States supporting C-V2X/LTE-V2X considered discriminatory. As a result, EU-wide C-ITS proceeds without a binding regulation. Interoperability is instead achieved through voluntary harmonisation via the C-Roads platform and industry consortia. 2010 ITS Directive Legal basis for delegated acts 2016 C-ITS Strategy COM(2016) 766 — 30 Nov 2016 2019 Delegated Reg. rejected Council objection — technology lock-in Policy Timeline 1 August 2010 — ITS Directive 2010/40/EU : Framework Directive adopted, empowering the Commission to adopt delegated acts in four priority areas. Priority Area IV covers linking the vehicle with the transport infrastructure, encompassing V2V, V2I and I2I cooperative systems. Article 6 grants authority to adopt specifications for compatibility, interoperability and continuity. This directive is the legal foundation for all subsequent C-ITS delegated acts. 2 November 2014 — C-ITS Platform launched (Phase I) : The Commission established the C-ITS Platform as an expert group bringing together Member States, vehicle manufacturers, road operators, telecom operators, service providers, and local/regional authorities. Phase I ran until January 2016 and produced a unanimous final report. 3 January 2016 — C-ITS Platform Phase I Final Report : The report recommended a "Day 1" service list for coordinated deployment, a common security/PKI trust model, a hybrid communication approach, and guiding principles for access to in-vehicle data. A Cost Benefit Analysis (the Ricardo / DG MOVE study) found benefit-cost ratios of 2–8 by 2030. 4 July 2016 — C-ITS Platform Phase II begins; C-Roads launched : The Commission starts Phase II of the expert group (July 2016 – September 2017) to develop concrete implementation conditions. Simultaneously, the C-Roads platform — a joint initiative of Member States and road operators — is launched to harmonise deployment specifications and test cross-border interoperability. C-Roads is co-funded through the Connecting Europe Facility (CEF). 5 30 November 2016 — EU C-ITS Strategy COM(2016) 766 : The Commission publishes "A European strategy on Cooperative Intelligent Transport Systems, a milestone towards cooperative, connected and automated mobility." It defines the Day 1 and Day 1.5 service lists, endorses a hybrid communication approach (ITS-G5 + cellular), commits to a PKI-based security framework, and announces the intention to adopt a delegated act by 2018 under the ITS Directive. 6 September 2017 — C-ITS Platform Phase II Final Report : Nine working groups produce recommendations on security/PKI, data protection/GDPR, compliance assessment, hybrid communication, urban C-ITS, business models, road safety, physical and digital infrastructure, and enhanced traffic management. The report explicitly supports the forthcoming delegated act. 7 January 2019 — Draft Delegated Regulation C(2019) 1789 : The Commission tables the draft regulation supplementing Directive 2010/40/EU, mandating ITS-G5 system profiles for vehicle and roadside C-ITS stations, a mandatory EU C-ITS Security Credential Management System (EU CCMS) based on PKI, and CE marking for C-ITS stations. It would apply from 31 December 2019. 8 2019 — Council Rejects the Delegated Regulation : A qualified majority of Member States objects, citing technology neutrality concerns. Countries and industry groups backing C-V2X/LTE-V2X argue the draft effectively locks in ITS-G5, pre-empting 5G cellular V2X and violating the principle of technology neutrality. The regulation is withdrawn. No binding EU C-ITS delegated act enters into force. 9 2020 onwards — C-Roads-led voluntary harmonisation & CCAM direction : Without a binding act, the C-Roads platform and the Car2Car Communication Consortium (C2CCC) publish harmonised service specifications and system profiles (C-Roads Release 2.0, October 2021). The Commission's Joint Research Centre (JRC) operates the EU CCMS PKI infrastructure voluntarily. The policy focus shifts toward Cooperative, Connected and Automated Mobility (CCAM) for the next generation. ITS Directive 2010/40/EU — the Legal Basis Directive 2010/40/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council (7 July 2010) provides the framework for deploying Intelligent Transport Systems in road transport and at interfaces with other modes. It is the primary legal instrument enabling the Commission to set binding technical specifications for ITS services through delegated acts. Article 2(1) identifies four priority areas. Priority Area IV — "Linking the vehicle with the transport infrastructure" — covers V2V, V2I and I2I cooperative systems. The ITS Directive's Annex I, point 4, specifies that actions in this area include defining measures to integrate ITS applications on an open in-vehicle platform and to progress cooperative systems. Article 6 empowers the Commission to adopt specifications (through delegated acts under Article 290 TFEU) ensuring compatibility, interoperability and continuity for the deployment and operational use of ITS applications and services. The Commission stressed in the 2016 Strategy that it would "consider using the ITS Directive 2010/40/EU" to adopt delegated acts by 2018 covering service continuity, security of communications, GDPR implementation in C-ITS, a hybrid communication approach, interoperability, and compliance assessment. Two earlier delegated regulations were already adopted under this Directive: Delegated Regulation (EU) 886/2013 on road-safety-related minimum universal traffic information, and Delegated Regulation (EU) 2015/962 on EU-wide real-time traffic information services. The C-ITS delegated act would have been the third major instrument, but it was never adopted. ● Relation to other legal instruments The ITS Directive sits alongside the Radio Equipment Directive 2014/53/EU (which C-ITS stations must comply with), GDPR (EU) 2016/679 (applicable to personal data in C-ITS messages), and Commission Decision 2008/671/EC (harmonising the 5 875–5 905 MHz frequency band for safety-related ITS applications in Europe). The 2016 EU C-ITS Strategy — COM(2016) 766 Adopted on 30 November 2016, the Communication "A European strategy on Cooperative Intelligent Transport Systems, a milestone towards cooperative, connected and automated mobility" (COM(2016) 766) is the central policy document of the EU's pre-deployment phase. It responds to the Declaration of Amsterdam (April 2016) in which European transport ministers called for a European strategy on cooperative, connected and automated vehicles. Vision and rationale The strategy identifies a risk of a fragmented internal market: without a common EU framework, investments and regulatory frameworks would not converge, jeopardising the 2019 deployment target that industry (led by the Car2Car Communication Consortium) had announced. The strategy estimated that Day 1 services, if deployed interoperably across Europe, would produce a benefit-cost ratio of up to 3 to 1 based on cumulative costs and benefits from 2018 to 2030 — and that slow initial uptake would reduce overall benefits due to weak network effects. Day 1 and Day 1.5 service lists The strategy defines two tiers of priority services for deployment from 2019: Tier Service Category Day 1 Slow or stationary vehicle(s) & traffic ahead warning Hazardous location Day 1 Road works warning Hazardous location Day 1 Weather conditions Hazardous location Day 1 Emergency brake light Hazardous location Day 1 Emergency vehicle approaching Hazardous location Day 1 Other hazards Hazardous location Day 1 In-vehicle signage Signage Day 1 In-vehicle speed limits Signage Day 1 Signal violation / intersection safety Signage Day 1 Traffic signal priority request by designated vehicles Signage Day 1 Green light optimal speed advisory Signage Day 1 Probe vehicle data Data collection Day 1 Shockwave damping Local hazard warning (ETSI) Day 1.5 Information on fuelling & charging stations for alternative fuel vehicles Info services Day 1.5 Vulnerable road user protection Safety Day 1.5 On-street parking management & information Urban Day 1.5 Off-street parking information Urban Day 1.5 Park & ride information Urban Day 1.5 Connected & cooperative navigation (first/last mile, parking, route advice) Urban Day 1.5 Traffic information & smart routing Efficiency C-ITS service deployment lists (COM(2016) 766) Day 1.5 services were deemed "generally mature" but lacking complete standards for large-scale deployment by 2019. The strategy asked the C-Roads platform and deployment initiatives to define "communication profiles" for Day 1 services and verify interoperability through cross-site testing. Hybrid communication policy The 2016 strategy endorsed a hybrid communication approach : combining complementary technologies to serve the full range of C-ITS use cases. The Commission identified the "most promising" mix as ETSI ITS-G5 (short-range, low-latency, operating in the 5.9 GHz band) combined with existing cellular networks (wide geographic coverage, large user group). The strategy stated that "initial deployment for short-range V2V and V2I will be based on technologies already available using this band," while 5G would be integrated under a complementarity principle in the longer term. Fewer than 5% of public consultation respondents disagreed with basing initial deployment on ITS-G5, and a large majority saw 5G playing an important role long-term. This apparent consensus would fracture by 2019. Security and PKI direction The strategy called for "a common security and certificate policy for C-ITS deployment in Europe" based on Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) . It committed the Commission to publishing guidance on the European C-ITS security and certificate policy in 2017 and stated that the Commission would "analyse the roles and responsibilities of the European C-ITS Trust Model." Full PKI architecture details are covered on the PKI & Trust page. Privacy and data protection The strategy acknowledged that data broadcast by C-ITS vehicles "will, in principle, qualify as personal data." It pointed to the upcoming GDPR (applicable from May 2018) and called for data protection by design and by default, data protection impact assessments (DPIAs), and transparent consent mechanisms. sectionTitle: The C-ITS Platform — Stakeholder Expert Group
text: The C-ITS Platform — Stakeholder Expert Group Launched in November 2014 as a Commission Expert Group, the C-ITS Platform provided a structured dialogue between the Commission, public stakeholders (Member State ministries, road authorities, cities via POLIS), and private stakeholders (vehicle manufacturers, equipment manufacturers, road operators, telecom operators, service providers). It operated in two phases. Phase I (November 2014 – January 2016) Phase I produced a unanimous final report in January 2016, recommending: a Day 1 service list; a common security trust model; a hybrid communication approach; guiding principles for access to in-vehicle data; and a detailed analysis of privacy and data protection as a basis for GDPR compliance work. Phase II (July 2016 – September 2017) Phase II deepened the technical and legal groundwork across nine working groups , divided into two tracks: "Phase I continued — support for deployment" and "Beyond C-ITS, towards CCAM." The September 2017 Final Report is the primary input to the draft Delegated Regulation. The Commission published the first version of the European C-ITS Certificate Policy in June 2017 as a direct output of the Security Working Group. Working Group Track Key Outcomes Security Phase I continued European C-ITS Certificate Policy (June 2017); security governance structure; recommendations for Commission to operate central PKI functions (CPA, TLM, CPOC) Data Protection & Privacy Phase I continued Legal basis analysis under GDPR Art.6; recommendation for EU legal instrument to provide a public-interest basis for data processing; DPIA template; data protection by design requirements Compliance Assessment Phase I continued Top-level methodology for testing and validation of C-ITS stations; roles and interaction framework; recommendation for progressive approach allowing Day 1 deployment while maintaining backward compatibility for future services Hybrid Communication Phase I continued Endorsed four policy principles: (1) uncompromised safety services for all users; (2) technology neutrality of spectrum; (3) efficient spectrum use; (4) 5G for longer-term CCAM. Only one meeting in Phase II — no specific new recommendations. Urban C-ITS Phase I continued Identified political, financial, technical and operational barriers to urban deployment; extended Day 1/1.5 services for urban use cases; urban automation scenarios Business Models Phase I continued Stakeholder perspective analysis; public-private partnership models; recommendations on roles and incentives along the C-ITS value chain Road Safety CCAM Priority C-ITS services from a safety perspective; Human Machine Interaction (HMI) guidelines; driver behaviour impacts; traffic rules adaptation Physical & Digital Infrastructure CCAM Infrastructure requirements for automation; connectivity for automated vehicles; positioning support (Galileo/EGNOS); handling complex traffic intersections Enhanced Traffic Management CCAM Cooperative Traffic Management concepts; Common Operational Picture; geo-fencing mechanisms; Network Level of Service definitions; digital Traffic Management Plans C-ITS Platform Phase II — working groups and key outcomes ● Access to in-vehicle data One contentious theme across both phases was access to in-vehicle data. The strategy identified "guiding principles" for this topic but acknowledged that further legal and technical analyses were needed. A dedicated Commission study was expected mid-2017. This issue intersects with the Applications layer, OEM business models, and competition policy — and remained unresolved in the draft Delegated Regulation.

The 2019 Draft Delegated Regulation C(2019) 1789 On 11 January 2019, the Commission submitted draft Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) …/… supplementing Directive 2010/40/EU with regard to the deployment and operational use of cooperative intelligent transport systems (reference Ares(2019)153204). Its stated purpose was to "create the minimal legal requirements for interoperability for C-ITS and to enable large-scale deployment of C-ITS systems and services from 2019." What the Regulation would have mandated System profiles (Annex II) Vehicle C-ITS stations and roadside C-ITS stations designed for short-range communication (5 855–5 925 MHz) must comply with ITS-G5-based system profiles. These are the harmonised profiles developed jointly by C-Roads and the Car2Car Communication Consortium. Each station must send messages enabling at least one C-ITS priority service (Annex I) and must be compatible with all priority services. EU C-ITS Security Credential Management System (EU CCMS) All C-ITS stations must enrol in and comply with the EU CCMS before being put in service. The EU CCMS implements PKI using pseudonym certificates (Authorisation Tickets, issued by an Authorisation Authority) and enrolment credentials (issued by an Enrolment Authority). Root CAs are listed in the European Certificate Trust List (ECTL), managed by the Trust List Manager (TLM). Until dedicated entities are established, the Commission (JRC + DG MOVE) acts as Certificate Policy Authority, TLM, and C-ITS Point of Contact (CPOC). Certificate and security policy (Annex III + Annex IV) Detailed PKI certificate policy (derived from IETF RFC 3647 framework) and information security management requirements (ISO/IEC 27001-based). Pseudonym certificates for mobile stations must ensure anonymity: Authorisation Tickets must not contain any names or information linking the station to a real identity. Certificate updates must reach C-ITS stations within one week of ECTL publication under normal operating conditions. CE marking and conformity assessment Manufacturers must draw up technical documentation, perform a conformity assessment, and affix CE marking before placing C-ITS stations on the market. Technical documentation and the EU declaration of conformity must be kept for 15 years. GDPR alignment The Regulation explicitly states it cannot by itself create a legal basis for personal data processing. Data controllers remain bound by GDPR Art.6. Personal data must not be re-used for commercial purposes or law enforcement without a separate lawful basis. The principle of data minimisation applies; data must not be stored longer than necessary. Entry into force Article 34 specified the Regulation would apply from 31 December 2019. ● Delegated Regulation REJECTED by Council — 2019 The Council of the EU exercised its right of objection under Article 290 TFEU. A sufficient number of Member States voted against the draft, primarily on the grounds of technology neutrality . The draft's Annex II system profiles were based on ITS-G5 (ETSI 802.11p / IEEE 802.11p), which critics argued would disadvantage C-V2X/LTE-V2X (3GPP Rel. 14 and beyond) and foreclose 5G-based short-range C-ITS communication. France, Germany, and several automotive-sector Member States, along with parts of the telecom industry organised in the 5G Automotive Association (5GAA, formed 2016), opposed the lock-in. The Regulation was never published in the Official Journal and never entered into force. Consequence: EU C-ITS has no binding harmonisation law. Deployment proceeds on a voluntary basis, steered by C-Roads platform harmonised specifications, C2CCC system profiles, and the Commission-operated EU CCMS PKI infrastructure.

sectionTitle: The ITS-G5 vs C-V2X Policy Tension
text: The ITS-G5 vs C-V2X Policy Tension The technology-neutrality dispute is the defining political fault-line in EU C-ITS policy. Understanding it requires distinguishing the two technology families: Dimension ITS-G5 (ETSI / IEEE 802.11p) C-V2X / LTE-V2X (3GPP) Standards basis ETSI EN 302 663, ETSI ITS-G5 stack; derived from IEEE 802.11p (Wi-Fi variant) 3GPP Release 14 (LTE-V2X PC5 interface); evolution to 5G NR-V2X in Release 16 Frequency band 5 875–5 925 MHz (ITS band, harmonised by Commission Decision 2008/671/EC) Same 5.9 GHz ITS band for direct (sidelink, PC5) mode; cellular uplink/downlink for network mode Latency profile Very low latency for direct V2V; no cellular infrastructure required Comparable low latency in direct mode; cellular mode adds network round-trip Infrastructure dependency None for V2V; RSU for V2I None for PC5 direct mode; cellular network needed for Uu interface services EU deployment status (2019) Deployed in C-Roads pilots, C2CCC system profiles, early OEM series production Prototypes and trials; 5GAA formed 2016; deployment starting later Commission 2016 position Endorsed as baseline for Day 1 initial deployment Acknowledged as future technology; 5G complementarity principle Post-rejection outcome Remains de facto standard in EU C-Roads deployments C-Roads exploring multi-technology profiles; both coexist ITS-G5 vs C-V2X short-range communication — policy comparison The Commission's 2016 Strategy was careful to describe ITS-G5 as the choice for "initial deployment" only, stressing that "C-ITS messages should be unaware of, and thus flexible about the communication technology used, easing the inclusion of future technologies (e.g. 5G and satellite communication) into the hybrid communication mix." However, when the 2019 draft Delegated Regulation specified ITS-G5-only system profiles in its Annex II (because ITS-G5 was the only mature, tested, standardised technology for short-range C-ITS at the time), this was interpreted as de facto mandating ITS-G5 and foreclosing LTE-V2X/5G. The Council objection followed. The Phase II Platform report's Hybrid Communication Working Group had already articulated the tension: it endorsed "technology neutrality of spectrum use" as a guiding principle while also acknowledging that backwards interoperability with already-deployed ITS-G5 stations was essential, given the long lifetime of vehicles. See also the Access Layer page for the technical comparison.

sectionTitle: Security & PKI Trust Model — Policy Dimension
text: Security & PKI Trust Model — Policy Dimension Across both C-ITS Platform phases, security governance was the single most complex policy topic. The challenge was creating a pan-European PKI that is simultaneously: technically robust (pseudonymity, frequent key rotation, no tracking), governable (clear roles for public and private entities), legally sound (consistent with GDPR), and operationally feasible for tens of millions of vehicles. C-ITS Certificate Policy Authority (CPA) Governance body — Commission acts as interim CPA ▼ Trust List Manager (TLM) Signs ECTL; Commission = interim TLM C-ITS Point of Contact (CPOC) Publishes ECTL; Commission = interim CPOC ▼ European Certificate Trust List (ECTL) Root CA (national / industry) + EU Root CA (operated by JRC) ▼ Enrolment Authority (EA) Issues Enrolment Credentials (EC) Authorisation Authority (AA) Issues Authorisation Tickets (AT) — pseudonym certs ▼ C-ITS Station (vehicle / RSU / personal) Uses AT for message signing — no persistent identity visible EU C-ITS trust model — PKI hierarchy The Certificate Policy (Annex III of the draft Delegated Regulation, first published June 2017) is structured around IETF RFC 3647. Key policy provisions include: The ECTL is updated on a maximum three-month cycle; C-ITS stations must receive updates within one week of publication under normal operating conditions. Authorisation Tickets (pseudonym certificates) must not contain any name or information that may link the station to its real identity — ensuring unlinkability for privacy. Root CAs may be operated by governmental or private organisations; an EU Root CA (JRC) is available for entities not wishing to set up their own. Cryptographic requirements mandate signature algorithms at ECDSA level with specified key lengths, with a crypto-agility requirement to adapt to future algorithm changes. Compliance audits by accredited PKI auditors are mandatory for all CAs listed in the ECTL. Even without the Delegated Regulation entering into force, the Commission (JRC) operates the EU CCMS infrastructure voluntarily. The CPOC protocol version 1.2 (December 2021) defines Level 0 (testing), Level 1 (intermediate operational), and Level 2 (full CP compliance) enrolment tiers, allowing early deployments to participate before achieving full compliance. See the PKI & Trust page for full technical details.

CCAM — The Next Policy Generation Both the 2017 Phase II report and subsequent EU policy have reframed C-ITS within the broader concept of Cooperative, Connected and Automated Mobility (CCAM) . The Platform's Phase II working groups on Physical & Digital Infrastructure, Enhanced Traffic Management, and Road Safety explicitly considered the requirements of higher levels of automation (SAE L3–L5). From C-ITS to CCAM The Phase II Platform concluded that "the ultimate goal is the full convergence of all developments under CCAM, making use of the digitisation of transport." C-ITS Day 1 services are the foundation; CCAM extends toward sensor-sharing (collective perception), manoeuvre coordination, and infrastructure-guided automation. See Overview . C-Roads as the Operational Hub In the absence of a binding delegated act, C-Roads became the de facto harmonisation body. Its release process (Release 2.0, October 2021) governs V2I service specifications, test procedures, and cross-border interoperability validation. EUR 199 million has been invested in C-ITS across 16 Member States (of which EUR 107 million via CEF). See C-Roads . EU EIP Recommendations (2022) The EU EIP sub-activity on C-ITS Deployment Support (2016–2021) concluded with 12 recommendations for road authorities: including multiyear budget planning, engagement with standardisation and profiling, IT security/privacy compliance, and integrating C-ITS into day-to-day traffic management operations. International Dimension The 2016 Strategy called for international cooperation with Australia, Japan, Singapore, the US, and through G7 transport minister declarations. The absence of a binding EU act complicates alignment with non-EU markets. See Global for US, Japanese, and Korean policy comparisons.

Global Standards Global C-ITS: US, ISO & SAE Vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication is not a purely European invention. The United States built a parallel — and in many ways earlier — ecosystem on SAE message sets, IEEE WAVE protocols, and a 5.9 GHz DSRC radio layer that predates ITS-G5 by several years. International standardisation through ISO TC 204 bridges both worlds. This page maps the US/global stack against the European one, explains the security architectures, and traces the FCC's controversial 2020 decision to reallocate DSRC spectrum and mandate a transition to C-V2X. SAE J2735_202409 SAE J2945/1 IEEE 1609.2 IEEE 1609.3 IEEE 1609.4 IEEE 802.11p IEEE 802.11bd ISO 21217 ISO 19091 DOT HS 812 014 Two Roads to V2X The US and Europe attacked the same problem — cooperative road safety — from almost the same starting point (5.9 GHz spectrum, ad-hoc broadcast, low latency) but through separate standards bodies and with different institutional histories. The result is two ecosystems that are functionally equivalent at the application level yet wire-incompatible at the radio security and message-encoding layers. Understanding the differences matters for three practical reasons: Vehicle OEMs sell globally and must decide which stack (or both) to equip. Infrastructure operators in border regions or on internationally operating corridors face interoperability gaps. Standards bodies (ISO, CEN, ETSI, SAE, IEEE) are actively harmonising — knowing the seams is prerequisite to closing them. ● Same physics, different protocols Both ecosystems transmit at 5.9 GHz, generate cooperative awareness approximately 10 times per second, and rely on PKI-signed certificates to authenticate messages. The divergence lies in message encoding (ASN.1 UPER formats differ), certificate formats (IEEE 1609.2 profiles vs. ETSI TS 103 097 profiles), and security management infrastructure (SCMS vs. CCMS). SAE J2735: The US Message Set Dictionary SAE J2735_202409 V2X Message Set Dictionary (latest release September 2024, preceded by 2023 and 2020 editions) is the normative ASN.1 specification for every V2X message in the US. It covers messages for vehicles, pedestrians, infrastructure, and emergency services — the rough equivalent of all ETSI facility-layer specifications combined into one document. A note on compatibility: J2735-2024 is backwards-compatible with the 2020 edition, but the 2023 release introduced a break, so care is needed when mixing firmware versions on RSUs and OBUs. Message Acronym US function ETSI equivalent Basic Safety Message BSM Periodic vehicle kinematic broadcast (position, speed, heading, acceleration, size) CAM Signal Phase and Timing SPaT Current and future signal states per movement at an intersection SPATEM Map Data MAP Intersection geometry: lanes, approaches, egresses, connectivity MAPEM Traveler Information Message TIM General road-user advisories: speed limits, closures, events; anchored to geographic region IVIM / DENM (partial) Roadside Alert RSA Hazard and event notifications from RSUs (analogue of event-triggered DENM) DENM Personal Safety Message PSM VRU (pedestrian, cyclist) periodic awareness broadcast VAM Signal Request / Status Message SRM / SSM In-vehicle request to extend/hold a green phase; RSU status reply SREM / SSEM Collective Perception Message (SAE J3224 SDSM) CPM Object list from sensor-equipped vehicle or RSU (emerging — SAE J3224 Sensor Data Sharing Message) CPM (ETSI) Key SAE J2735 messages and their ETSI equivalents BSM structure highlights The BSM is the SAE analogue of the CAM . It is transmitted at up to 10 Hz. Part I (mandatory) carries: message count, temporary ID (128-bit pseudonym, rotated for privacy), DSRC seconds-of-minute, latitude/longitude (1/10 microdegree resolution), elevation, positional accuracy (semi-major/minor axes), transmission state, speed (0.02 m/s LSB), heading (0.0125 ° LSB), steering angle, acceleration set (longitudinal, lateral, vertical, yaw rate), brake system status, vehicle size. Part II (optional extensions) adds event flags, path history, path prediction, exterior lights, and additional sensor data. The temporary ID rotation interval is security-policy-driven (SCMS pseudonym certificate lifetime, typically minutes to hours). ● BSM vs. CAM: key structural differences The CAM uses ETSI ASN.1 UPER encoding with explicit container nesting (ITS PDU Header → CoopAwareness → BasicContainer + HighFrequencyContainer + optional LowFrequencyContainer). The BSM uses SAE ASN.1 encoding with a flat Part I + optional Part II blob. Field precision is similar but not identical (e.g. heading resolution differs). Neither message is on-wire compatible with the other, even though they carry largely the same vehicle physics. SPaT and MAP ISO 19091 V2I intersection using SPaT/MAP adopts SAE J2735 SPaT and MAP as its normative payload — making these messages a genuine international standard for signalised intersection communication, not just a US one. The EU MAPEM and SPATEM facility messages are built on the same conceptual model; ETSI adapted the message containers for the ITS-S architecture but the intersection geometry and signal-state encoding are directly derived from J2735. SAE J2945: System & Application Requirements Where J2735 defines message syntax, the SAE J2945/1 On-Board System Requirements for V2V Safety series defines system-level performance requirements — how often to transmit, minimum receiver sensitivity, congestion control, security credential handling, and application logic. J2945/1 (On-Board System Requirements for V2V Safety Communications, light vehicles) is the primary reference for BSM generation and corresponds functionally to ETSI EN 302 637-2 CAM in the EU. J2945/1 On-board requirements for BSM transmission and reception; congestion control (DCC-like); security credential lifecycle for light vehicles. J2945/2 Safety awareness applications built on BSM. J2945/3 Weather-related CV applications. J2945/4 Road safety applications (work zone, school zone, emergency). J2945/5 Service-specific permissions (SSP) framework — what a certificate is authorised to sign. J2945/6 Performance requirements for cooperative adaptive cruise control (CACC) and platooning. J2945/9 Vulnerable road user (VRU) safety using PSM. IEEE WAVE: The US Protocol Stack The Wireless Access in Vehicular Environments (WAVE) standard family (IEEE 1609.x) plays the same role in the US that ETSI EN 302 663 ITS-G5 access layer + ETSI EN 302 636-4 GeoNetworking + ETSI EN 302 636-5 BTP play in Europe: it sits between the 802.11p radio and the SAE J2735 application messages. It uses 10 MHz channels (half-clocked 802.11a OFDM) to tolerate the fast Doppler spreads of vehicular channels. The maximum data rate is 27 Mbit/s (64-QAM, 3/4 coding); typical safety message operation uses 6 Mbit/s BPSK. This is the radio basis of both US DSRC and European ITS-G5 — the two are interoperable at the PHY/MAC level. It is the upper layers (security, networking, messages) where they diverge. IEEE 802.11bd (Next-Generation V2X, NGV) is the 802.11p successor. It adds LDPC coding, MIMO support, extended range mode, and 20 MHz channel operation while maintaining backward interoperability with 802.11p devices on 10 MHz channels. 802.11bd is the WLAN counterpart to 5G NR-V2X (3GPP Rel-16 PC5 sidelink), giving the DSRC/ITS-G5 ecosystem a future technology path analogous to C-V2X's NR-V2X roadmap. 10 MHz 802.11p channel width 5.850–5.925 GHz (US original 75 MHz band) 27 Mbit/s 802.11p peak data rate 6 Mbit/s BPSK typical for BSM safety messages 300–500 m Typical DSRC/ITS-G5 range Up to 1 km line-of-sight; C-V2X ~20–30% more Security Trust Models: US SCMS vs. EU CCMS Both regions require PKI-backed signed certificates so that every received V2X message can be cryptographically verified as coming from a legitimate device. The architecture of each trust model is very similar in principle. The implementation , governance , and certificate format differ significantly. same concept, different registry (ISO 17419 vs. IEEE 1609.12) Deployment model Centralised US-national SCMS operators; CV pilots (NYC, Tampa, Wyoming) used shared SCMS Federated: each member state or road operator runs own EA/AA, rooted in EU CPOC trust list Interoperability IEEE 1609.2 cert format can be used globally; SCMS not interoperable with CCMS without a gateway CCMS certs not readable by WAVE stack without adaptation; cross-recognition requires bilateral agreements SCMS (US) vs. CCMS (EU) trust model comparison ● Cross-Atlantic certificate incompatibility A vehicle with a CCMS Authorisation Ticket cannot authenticate its messages to a US RSU running the WAVE stack, and vice versa. The certificate formats share the same underlying ASN.1 structure (IEEE 1609.2) but differ in profile choices and trust-anchor registries. Harmonisation is an active topic in ISO TC 204 and ETSI TC ITS. SCMS component architecture The SCMS was designed and described in the NHTSA V2V Readiness Report (DOT HS 812 014, August 2014) and subsequently refined through the three US Connected Vehicle Pilot programmes (New York City, Tampa FL, Wyoming). Key components: Root CA Apex trust anchor; offline; signs intermediate CA certificates. Enrolment CA (ECA) Issues Long-Term Certificates to authenticated OBUs/RSUs during device provisioning. Pseudonym CA (PCA) Issues batches of short-lived Pseudonym Certificates to vehicles; certificates rotated to prevent tracking. Linkage Authorities (LA1, LA2) Two independent authorities that jointly compute linkage values enabling revocation of misbehaving devices without revealing device identity to either authority alone (butterfly-key scheme). Misbehaviour Authority (MA) Receives misbehaviour reports, decides on revocation, coordinates with LAs. Policy Generator (PG) Maintains certificate policy, SSP definitions, and approved PSID values. Location Obscurer Proxy (LOP) Prevents the PCA from learning the geographic location implied by certificate requests.

sectionTitle: FCC 5.9 GHz Reallocation & the DSRC-to-C-V2X Shift
text: FCC 5.9 GHz Reallocation & the DSRC-to-C-V2X Shift The US originally allocated the entire 75 MHz band from 5.850 to 5.925 GHz exclusively to DSRC for ITS safety (1999 FCC order). After more than 20 years of limited DSRC deployment — the FCC noted that "DSRC has barely been deployed, in the more than 20 years since the adoption of DSRC, meaning this spectrum has been largely unused" — the FCC issued a major reallocation in November 2020 (FCC-20-164). ● FCC 2020 spectrum reallocation — the key numbers The FCC repurposed 45 MHz (5.850–5.895 GHz) from DSRC to unlicensed Wi-Fi (UNII-4), retaining only 30 MHz (5.895–5.925 GHz) for ITS operations. Critically, the rules mandate that this 30 MHz band must use C-V2X technology at the end of a transition period, effectively retiring DSRC/802.11p in the US. Transition timeline 1 Pre-2020 — DSRC era: 75 MHz reserved exclusively for DSRC; three major USDOT-funded CV pilot programmes (NYC 4,000 OBUs + 550 RSUs; Tampa 1,000 vehicles + 47 RSUs; Wyoming 400 fleet OBUs + 75 RSUs) deployed 802.11p / SAE J2735 / IEEE 1609 hardware. Michigan Safety Pilot 2012-2014 put V2X devices in 2,800 vehicles across 75 miles of roadway. 2 November 2020 — FCC-20-164: Lower 45 MHz reallocated to unlicensed use. Upper 30 MHz retained for ITS; DSRC operators given 12 months to vacate the lower band, then a further period to migrate upper-band operations to C-V2X. Guard band between unlicensed Wi-Fi and new ITS band removed, raising OOBE interference concerns. 3 2021–2022 — Dual-mode bridge: Existing DSRC RSU/OBU hardware not software-upgradeable to C-V2X (different chipsets). Dual-mode DSRC/C-V2X devices (e.g. Applied Information AI-500) emerged. Tennessee DOT deployed them on the MLK Smart Corridor in Chattanooga. UTC experiments showed C-V2X achieved 514 m max range vs. 427 m for DSRC, with lower packet loss under reduced line-of-sight. 4 Ongoing concern — 30 MHz sufficiency: The US DOT 5.9 GHz Spectrum Team conducted real-world LTE-V2X radio performance tests. Early results showed potential congestion issues vs. DSRC in dense traffic. The current 30 MHz may not be sufficient for fully cooperative automated vehicle scenarios; a FCC Second Report and Order is expected to address this. DSRC vs. C-V2X technology comparison Property DSRC / IEEE 802.11p C-V2X (LTE-V2X Rel-14/15 PC5) Radio standard IEEE 802.11p — OFDM, 10 MHz channels, 5.9 GHz 3GPP LTE PC5 sidelink — SC-FDM, 10 MHz channels, 5.9 GHz MAC access CSMA/CA — contention-based, fully decentralised Sensing-Based Semi-Persistent Scheduling (SB-SPS) — autonomous resource selection (Mode 4) Latency (direct comm) 1–5 ms 1–20 ms (varies with scheduling period) Range (line-of-sight) 300–1000 m (DSRC) ~20–30% greater than DSRC per UTC Chattanooga tests Synchronisation Loose asynchronous; 8 µs symbol duration Tight synchronous; ~70 µs symbol duration; GNSS sync required for Mode 4 Error correction coding Convolutional code Turbo code + HARQ — better performance in multipath fading Concurrent transmissions Cannot do concurrent transmissions (CSMA contention) SC-FDM supports concurrent transmissions Message set SAE J2735 (shared) SAE J2735 (same — technology-agnostic) Security IEEE 1609.2 / SCMS (same for both) IEEE 1609.2 / SCMS (same — technology-agnostic) V2N (network path) Not supported by 802.11p itself Supported via LTE/5G uplink to network in indirect mode OEM adoption examples Toyota (Japan 2015), GM Cadillac (US 2017), VW Golf 8 (EU 2019) Ford, Daimler, Stellantis endorsing C-V2X; Qualcomm C-V2X chipsets shipping 2021+ DSRC (IEEE 802.11p / WAVE) vs. C-V2X (LTE-V2X PC5) — key differences ● Dual-mode devices as a bridge strategy Dual-mode RSUs and OBUs (supporting both 802.11p DSRC and LTE-V2X on the same hardware) allow agencies to serve legacy DSRC vehicles while accepting C-V2X devices. TDOT tested Applied Information AI-500 dual-mode RSUs on the MLK Smart Corridor in Chattanooga with promising results. Hawaii DOT deployed dual-radio DSRC/C-V2X units at 36 traffic signals on a 5-mile arterial in Honolulu.

sectionTitle: NHTSA V2V Readiness Work — DOT HS 812 014
text: NHTSA V2V Readiness Work — DOT HS 812 014 DOT HS 812 014 (August 2014, ~327 pages) is the foundational US government readiness assessment for V2V deployment. Published by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), it evaluated technical, legal, policy, privacy, and economic dimensions of a potential V2V mandate based on data from the Michigan Safety Pilot Model Deployment (2012–2014, 2,800 vehicles, Ann Arbor MI). 2,800 Vehicles in Michigan Safety Pilot 2012–2014, Ann Arbor, 27 RSUs, 75 miles roadway 49–1,083 Lives potentially saved annually IMA + LTA applications alone at fleet saturation $341–350 Estimated OBU cost per vehicle 2020 forecast at production scale 25,000–592,000 Crashes preventable annually IMA + LTA at full fleet penetration Key findings from NHTSA's assessment (DOT HS 812 014): V2V functions work: BSM transmit/receive demonstrated at scale; SCMS provided trusted communications. Safety applications — Intersection Movement Assist (IMA), Left Turn Assist (LTA), Forward Collision Warning (FCW), Electronic Emergency Brake Light (EEBL) — proved effective in mitigating potential crashes but needed refinement before performance standards could be finalised. NHTSA confirmed legal authority to mandate V2V devices in new light vehicles and commercial vehicles already on the road. Privacy is addressable through pseudonym certificate rotation; the report endorsed the SCMS butterfly-key approach. SCMS identified as critical shared infrastructure requiring governance decisions on liability and long-term funding. New York City CVPD 4,000 OBUs on taxis, buses, cars; 550 RSUs in Manhattan and Brooklyn CBD. Applications include vehicle-turning warning, red-light violation warning, pedestrian mobile signal, and oversize vehicle compliance. Tampa (THEA) CVPD 1,000 privately-owned vehicles, 8 streetcars, 10 regional buses; 47 RSUs. Six use-cases including wrong-way entry detection, pedestrian safety, Transit Signal Priority, and streetcar conflict warnings. Wyoming (WYDOT) CVPD 400 fleet OBUs on I-80 — one of the busiest freight corridors (30–55% truck traffic); 75 RSUs. Applications: Forward Collision Warning, Work Zone Warning, Spot Weather Impact Warning, Distress Notification.

ISO TC 204: International ITS Standards ISO Technical Committee 204 (Intelligent Transport Systems) is the primary international standards body for ITS architecture, protocols, and applications. Its work provides the conceptual and architectural framework that both the EU (via ETSI and CEN) and the US (via SAE and IEEE) reference — often adopting ISO specs as normative references rather than rewriting them. Standard Scope EU / US relevance ISO 21217 ITS-S Architecture ITS station (ITS-S) reference architecture; management, security, and facilities layers; CALM (Communications Access for Land Mobiles) framework Normative basis for ETSI EN 302 665 ITS-S architecture; referenced by US WAVE architecture (IEEE 1609.0) ISO 19091 V2I SPaT/MAP Using V2I communications for signalised intersection management; normatively adopts SAE J2735 SPaT and MAP messages International adoption of US SAE messages; ETSI SPATEM/MAPEM are EU profiles of ISO 19091 ISO/TS 19321 In-Vehicle Information (IVI) data structures for sign / speed limit content Basis of EU IVIM payload (ETSI TS 103 301) ISO 17419 ITS Application Identifier (ITS-AID) registry — globally unique application identifiers Parallels IEEE 1609.12 PSID registry; cross-mapping between ITS-AID and PSID is an active harmonisation topic ISO 21210 IPv6 networking for ITS stations; router discovery and addressing Used in ETSI GeoNetworking IPv6 adaptation ISO 21218 Access technology support interfaces for ITS-S (ITS-G5, C-V2X, GNSS) Multi-access framework in EU hybrid V2X deployments ISO 24102-x ITS station management plane: configuration, monitoring, software update ETSI TS 102 636-6 management; WAVE station management ISO/SAE 21434 Road vehicles cybersecurity engineering (threat analysis, risk assessment, V-model process) Applies alongside C-ITS PKI in both regions; EU mandated via UNECE WP.29 R155 ISO 29281 Fast Networking and Transport Protocol (FNTP) — non-IP messaging for ITS-S EU non-IP path in GeoNetworking stack; less prevalent in US WAVE Key ISO TC 204 standards relevant to C-ITS / V2X The ISO / ETSI / SAE relationship ETSI and ISO operate under the Vienna Agreement (via CEN) for collaboration. In practice: ISO TC 204 produces the architectural and conceptual framework (ISO 21217 ITS-S architecture, ISO 19091 intersection management). ETSI TC ITS produces the European profile : concrete message encodings, parameter constraints, and deployment rules (EN 302 637-2 for CAM, TS 103 097 for security). SAE and IEEE produce the US profile : J2735 messages, J2945 performance requirements, 1609.x protocols. The ISO standard often references both: ISO 19091 normatively adopts J2735 SPaT/MAP; ISO 21217 is the normative basis for EN 302 665. ● ISO 21217 as the common root ETSI EN 302 665 and the US WAVE architecture (IEEE 1609.0) both claim alignment with ISO 21217. The layered model — access, networking and transport, facilities, applications, management, security — is the same across all three. Implementations diverge at the networking layer and below. ISO 21217 is the closest thing to a shared design document for V2X worldwide.

EU ↔ US Message Equivalence Despite wire incompatibility, every EU facility message has a functional US counterpart and vice versa. The table below shows the full cross-region mapping. Understanding these equivalences is essential for cross-border deployments, simulator interoperability testing, and future harmonisation work. Function ETSI EU message SAE / US message Harmonisation notes Periodic vehicle awareness CAM — EN 302 637-2 BSM — SAE J2735 + J2945/1 Both ~10 Hz; both use pseudonym certs; field precision similar but not identical; encoding incompatible on-wire Event / hazard notification DENM — EN 302 637-3 RSA (RSU-sourced) / TIM — SAE J2735 DENM is more richly structured (cause/sub-cause codes, geo-repetition rules); TIM/RSA cover similar event types with simpler structure Signal phase and timing SPATEM — ETSI TS 103 301 / ISO 19091 SPaT — SAE J2735, ISO 19091 SPATEM is an EU profile of SAE J2735 SPaT; closest to direct equivalence of any cross-region pair; a gateway needs only to re-encode the header Intersection topology MAPEM — ETSI TS 103 301 / ISO 19091 MAP (MapData) — SAE J2735, ISO 19091 MAPEM is an EU profile of SAE J2735 MAP; essentially the same ASN.1 structure with an ETSI ITS PDU header Infrastructure / static road info IVIM — ETSI TS 103 301 / ISO/TS 19321 TIM — SAE J2735 IVIM uses ISO/TS 19321 IVI data structures; TIM covers speed limits, closures, advisories with geographic anchoring Signal request / status SREM / SSEM — ETSI TS 103 301 SRM / SSM — SAE J2735 EU SREM/SSEM are direct profiles of SAE SRM/SSM; among the most directly harmonised pairs VRU / pedestrian awareness VAM — ETSI TS 103 300-3 PSM (Personal Safety Message) — SAE J2735, J2945/9 VAM carries VRU cluster and motion prediction info; PSM is simpler; not interoperable on-wire; functionally equivalent Collective perception CPM — ETSI TS 103 324 SDSM (Sensor Data Sharing Message) — SAE J3224 (emerging, 2024) Both carry perceived object lists from on-board sensors; SAE J3224 SDSM is still being standardised; functional alignment with ETSI CPM expected Security certificate format ETSI TS 103 097 certificate IEEE 1609.2 certificate ETSI TS 103 097 is a profile of IEEE 1609.2 — same ASN.1 base, different profile choices and trust registries; not directly interoperable without gateway adaptation Full EU (ETSI) ↔ US (SAE/IEEE) message equivalence ● SPaT/MAP: the closest cross-Atlantic pair SPaT and MAP messages are the most harmonised across regions. ISO 19091 adopted SAE J2735 SPaT/MAP normatively; ETSI TS 103 301 SPATEM/MAPEM then wraps the same ASN.1 payload in an ITS PDU header. A conversion gateway needs only to re-encode the header and adjust minor field constraints — far simpler than BSM ↔ CAM conversion, which requires remapping structurally different kinematic containers.

sectionTitle: US vs. EU Protocol Stack Side-by-Side
text: US vs. EU Protocol Stack Side-by-Side US Stack (WAVE / DSRC) Applications FCW, IMA, BSM apps, SPaT consumers, SCMS clients SAE J2735 Messages BSM, SPaT, MAP, TIM, RSA, PSM, SRM/SSM IEEE 1609.3 — WSMP WAVE Short Message Protocol (PSID-keyed routing) IEEE 1609.4 Multi-Channel Operation (CCH ch 172 / SCH) IEEE 1609.2 Security Signed / encrypted msgs; certificate verification IEEE 802.11p PHY/MAC 5.9 GHz, 10 MHz OCB channels, OFDM, up to 27 Mbit/s EU Stack (ITS-G5 / C-ITS) Applications ETSI Day 1/2 apps, GLOSA, EEBL, traffic light assist ETSI Facility Messages CAM, DENM, CPM, VAM, SPATEM, MAPEM, IVIM BTP + GeoNetworking EN 302 636-4/5; GeoBroadcast / Topologically Scoped ITS-G5 Channel Mgmt / DCC ETSI TS 102 724; Decentralised Congestion Control ETSI TS 103 097 Security Profile of IEEE 1609.2; CCMS AT-signed messages ITS-G5 / IEEE 802.11p PHY/MAC EN 302 663; 5.9 GHz, 10 MHz OCB, OFDM US WAVE stack (left) vs. EU ITS-G5 / C-ITS stack (right) — layer-by-layer The physical and MAC layers (802.11p) are identical — a US DSRC radio and an EU ITS-G5 radio decode each other's raw frames. The divergence begins at the networking layer: WSMP uses PSID-keyed broadcast; GeoNetworking uses geographic addressing. Security certificates share the same ASN.1 base (IEEE 1609.2) but have incompatible trust anchors and profile choices. Messages use different container structures. A cross-region gateway must therefore operate at the networking and facility layers, not the PHY/MAC.
